coreStoryFacts.text: Reading about all that damage, to both infrastructure and animals, inspired Sara Nozkova (pictured above on the left) to develop a wildlife-deterrent system that works differently from the sirens, lights, fences, falcons, and culling traditionally used to keep animals away from roads, train tracks, airports, and other infrastructure.

That work turned into Flox Intelligence , which spun out of KTH in 2020 and is one of the finalists at this year’s Startup Battlefield 200 pitch competition at TechCrunch Disrupt , taking place this year at Moscone West in San Francisco October 13-15.
Like autonomous vehicles, they use perception systems to sense their surroundings, but theirs are trained on wildlife behavior.

Nozkova says about 150 Flox devices are live in North America, Europe, and Australia at airfields and airport perimeters, road and rail corridors (especially fence ends and crossings along wildlife corridors), national parks, agricultural land, urban areas, mining sites, and critical infrastructure such as electrical substations.
The train, you see, had apparently hit a wild bison at full speed, and the impact damaged the engine so badly that it had to be towed away for repairs.

After spending 13 years working in transportation and autonomous vehicles, Nozkova had learned how quickly the systems we build to navigate roads and other controlled environments fail once nature enters the equation.
Flox also has OEM partnerships with companies that pay an annual fee to deploy its software on vehicles, like trains.

extraction.body: When I was eight, I remember our train to Mumbai ground to a halt with a great noise. When we started moving again, a good eight hours later, someone pointed out a mangled tail, of all things, hanging from a branch close to the tracks. The train, you see, had apparently hit a wild bison at full speed, and the impact damaged the engine so badly that it had to be towed away for repairs. For a long time, I thought such things only happened in places like rural India, but I learned a few years ago that wildlife and infrastructure do not mix anywhere on the planet. The FAA estimates that wildlife strikes have cost U.S. civil aviation about $272 million a year on average between 1990 and 2025. In France, the rail operator SNCF says wandering animals affect more than 8,000 trains across the country each year and are among its five leading causes of delays. In Brittany, 120 trains hit animals in 2023 alone, disrupting 660 services and causing more than 15,000 minutes of delays. Reading about all that damage, to both infrastructure and animals, inspired Sara Nozkova (pictured above on the left) to develop a wildlife-deterrent system that works differently from the sirens, lights, fences, falcons, and culling traditionally used to keep animals away from roads, train tracks, airports, and other infrastructure. “I was convinced the answer was not a louder deterrent,” she told TechCrunch. A motion sensor wakes the device when it detects movement, triggering a camera that uses on-device models to identify nearby animals. The device then emits a species-appropriate sound to scare them away. Nozkova says the system learns from experience, too, and varies its responses so animals don’t get habituated to repeated signals. sources.title: Sweden's Flox Intelligence raises €2.5 million to become a “digital shepherd” guiding wildlife away from danger - EU-Startups
passages: Flox Intelligence , a wildlife intelligence company building AI systems enabling infrastructure to prevent human-wildlife conflict, today announced a €2.5 million ($3 million) Seed+ round to accelerate deployments across North America.
It is building edge-based physical AI that can operate 24/7 in harsh environments, where decisions have to be made in seconds.
The company combines embedded systems, real-time sensing, and applied wildlife science to speak with animals in their own language.
“For decades, we’ve relied on reactive tools — from scare tactics to fences — that don’t scale, don’t learn, and don’t protect the corridors wildlife depends on.
For so many years, we have been fighting wildlife, but what if we could communicate with them instead?

“Flox Intelligence is building a future where critical infrastructure can proactively prevent conflict, where animal movement is respected and safer, and where people and wildlife can finally coexist.

The technology prevents collisions, damage, and disruption across critical infrastructure, including railways, airports, roads, agriculture, and industrial sites, and provides reporting through the Flox Wildlife Platform.
This keeps growing every year as humans take more space, wild animals are pushed closer to urban spaces, and transportation systems get faster, quieter, and harder to avoid.
Flox Intelligence was founded in 2020 by Nozkova and Tomas Becklin.
It was born out of an AI research lab at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm.
The company recently relocated its commercial headquarters to the US.
It is also helping DOT road networks where deer and bison collisions drive injuries, fatalities, and financial losses.
Flox Intelligence claims to be built on a different premise.
It has expanded its operations across the U.S. and Canada, grown its New York headquarters, and accelerated commercial deployments over the past few months.
Ford International Airport, WWF, KWS Group, Boliden, and Alstom.

The startup’s first commercial product, Edge, is an intelligent wildlife deterrent system built for harsh, real-world environments, engineered for multiple species, extreme weather, remote sites, limited connectivity, and long uptime.

Every deployment makes the next one smarter, and collectively, these deployments are building one of the world’s largest non-lethal wildlife datasets and windows into how wildlife moves, adapts, and survives alongside human infrastructure.

extraction.body: Flox Intelligence , a wildlife intelligence company building AI systems enabling infrastructure to prevent human-wildlife conflict, today announced a €2.5 million ($3 million) Seed+ round to accelerate deployments across North America. The round was led by Tilia Impact Ventures, with participation from Satgana, GENIUS NY (operated by CenterState CEO), J.O.S.S. and existing investors Unconventional Ventures and Almi Invest. Sara Nozkova , CEO and co-founder of Flox Intelligence, said, “The future of infrastructure safety will include wildlife intelligence by default. “For decades, we’ve relied on reactive tools — from scare tactics to fences — that don’t scale, don’t learn, and don’t protect the corridors wildlife depends on. For so many years, we have been fighting wildlife, but what if we could communicate with them instead? “Flox Intelligence is building a future where critical infrastructure can proactively prevent conflict, where animal movement is respected and safer, and where people and wildlife can finally coexist. Our goal is to make wildlife intelligence a standard layer of modern operations — and to lead that category globally.” Flox Intelligence was founded in 2020 by Nozkova and Tomas Becklin. It was born out of an AI research lab at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm. The company recently relocated its commercial headquarters to the US. Flox Intelligence is an AI-powered wildlife intelligence company that aims to create a world where humans and wildlife coexist. According to the company, it builds autonomous systems deployed on the edge that guide wildlife in real time using AI, bioacoustics, and applied wildlife science. The technology prevents collisions, damage, and disruption across critical infrastructure, including railways, airports, roads, agriculture, and industrial sites, and provides reporting through the Flox Wildlife Platform. The company claims to replace reactive, fragmented deterrents like scarecrows, pyrotechnics, gunshots, and fences with a modern, autonomous layer of prevention and learning at the edge. Every deployment makes the next one smarter, and collectively, these deployments are building one of the world’s largest non-lethal wildlife datasets and windows into how wildlife moves, adapts, and survives alongside human infrastructure. Flox Intelligence mentions that human-wildlife conflict is already a global multi-billion-euro problem. This keeps growing every year as humans take more space, wild animals are pushed closer to urban spaces, and transportation systems get faster, quieter, and harder to avoid. According to the company, existing tools do not scale and lack adaptive learning capabilities. Flox Intelligence claims to be built on a different premise. It is building edge-based physical AI that can operate 24/7 in harsh environments, where decisions have to be made in seconds. The company combines embedded systems, real-time sensing, and applied wildlife science to speak with animals in their own language. “In other words, it turns wildlife communication into actionable intelligence — enabling critical infrastructure to “speak” with wildlife and gently guide them away from high-risk zones before incidents happen,” mentioned Flox Intelligence. The startup’s first commercial product, Edge, is an intelligent wildlife deterrent system built for harsh, real-world environments, engineered for multiple species, extreme weather, remote sites, limited connectivity, and long uptime. It is always on, multi-species, multi-modal, and deployed at the edge. Flox Intelligence has already started shipping Edge pods to the front lines of human-wildlife conflict, including airports dealing with coyotes, deer, and bird strike risks, to rail corridors affected by large wildlife such as moose and bears. It is also helping DOT road networks where deer and bison collisions drive injuries, fatalities, and financial losses. Some other use cases of Edge include ranches and farms balancing predator-healthy ecosystems with livestock protection, and cities and public spaces that witness wildlife movement. The company reports that Edge has logged over 60,000 wildlife events across 27 species, and early deployments show measurable reductions in wildlife presence in high-risk zones. This funding follows Flox Intelligence’s Seed round in July last year. It has expanded its operations across the U.S. and Canada, grown its New York headquarters, and accelerated commercial deployments over the past few months. The fresh capital will be used by the company to accelerate deployments across North America. It will also support growing international demand for Flox Intelligence’s AI-powered wildlife deterrence platform across airports, rail corridors, road networks, and industrial sites. Flox Intelligence reports that it already works with major airports, departments of transportation, infrastructure owners, and mission-driven partners across North America and Europe. Its partners include the U.S. Department of Agriculture, GRR Gerald R. Ford International Airport, WWF, KWS Group, Boliden, and Alstom.

Interactive Brokers ( Nasdaq : IBKR), an automated global broker, announced the launch of cryptocurrency staking for eligible clients on October 13. The service allows clients to earn rewards on supported digital assets while managing their cryptocurrency alongside stocks, options, futures, and other instruments on the firm’s unified platform. According to the official announcement , eligible Interactive Brokers LLC clients can initially stake Ethereum through the Staking Dashboard in IBKR’s Client Portal. Clients can submit staking or unstaking requests and monitor pending activity. Rewards, when earned, are credited as additional staked cryptocurrency and may compound while the position remains staked. The launch expands Interactive Brokers’ existing cryptocurrency services. Product availability varies by Interactive Brokers affiliate and the client’s country of residence. The firm also cautioned that digital asset trading carries elevated risks and is intended for individuals with a high risk tolerance and the financial capacity to sustain losses. Prior to this, on August 4, digital asset firm Galaxy Digital and BNY announced that they were exploring a partnership to introduce staking capabilities within BNY’s Digital Asset Custody platform. According to the announcement at the time, Galaxy would support staking infrastructure for BNY and serve as a design partner for the bank’s broader digital asset platform. The staking offering was not yet available to clients and remained subject to regulatory review, with no launch timeline announced. sources.title: Apple’s HomeView ad is confusing to everyone except parents
passages: Apple’s ad introducing its new HomeView smart display is a little unusual.

Even if Apple didn’t need to do much to heighten the stakes of a family getting out the door, there is of course plenty of sleight of hand at work when it comes to making the HomeView appear so essential.

There’s also a microdrama about the daughter’s ride to school with a boyfriend nobody knew about that ends with everyone gathered around the HomeView watching the security camera feed of the two of them departing the porch.

When tech analyst Benedict Evans posted about the ad feeling stressful and confusing, CNET editor at large Bridget Carey chimed in to defend it, saying “It was exactly what my morning is like and it was the most real ad I’ve ever seen from Apple.” Others agreed, saying it “accurately captured” real life and that it “hit home,” no pun intended, at least I think.
Apple’s typical vibe is clean, simple, orderly; this commercial is chaos.

If the alternative is five people all interacting with their own phones, then the HomeView presents a different picture where everyone gets the essential information they need from one shared screen and stays more present.

extraction.body: Apple today announced HomeView, a $299 smart home display with a 7-inch screen that lets users control connected accessories, make FaceTime calls, and enjoy music and video content. But what about third-party apps? Here’s what Apple says. Apple says the new HomeView smart home display is “designed for life at home,” with a wide range of features for managing connected accessories, staying organized, and enjoying entertainment. That includes everything from controlling smart home devices and checking calendars to watching videos, listening to music, and making FaceTime calls. However, one question Apple’s announcement didn’t fully answer is the extent to which HomeView will support third-party apps. According to Apple, in addition to a selection of Apple apps, including Music, Podcasts, and Safari, HomeView will also support “compatible third-party audio and video apps from your iPhone for a familiar experience across devices.” Interestingly, the fine print for this feature differs between Apple’s HomeView marketing page and the product’s press release. The press release , however, includes an additional detail (emphasis ours): Subscription may be required to access some content and services. Some applications are not available in all areas. Select apps require a paired and compatible iPhone nearby. Some of Apple’s own first-party apps will also be available from the iPhone, the company notes. That includes Audiobooks, Apple Music Classical, News, and TV. Apple has yet to detail how the iPhone proximity requirement will work, and whether developers of apps in supported categories will need to take any additional steps to support HomeView. Not trying to be the negative Nancy here but does this actually look like a useful product that will sell much outside of the apple customer that needs to get anything they put out? I know some have talked in the past about wanting something in the kitchen but what does this do that an iPad can't do for those needs? If this came out 15+ years ago, I could see it catching on for awhile before people realized they could get other devices to do what it does better. Apple is usually good with knowing their markets so I guess we'll see. This just feels like it's going against the direction of everything else. Most desktop computer users went to laptops, tablets, and phones already meaning having a static device and going mobile...or so I thought. According ot Wired , “a handful of third-party media apps like Spotify are available, and developers can bring over existing CarPlay apps.” Wired adds that “if your iPhone already has one of these CarPlay apps installed, it can automatically appear on the HomeView after setup.” So it looks like HomeView’s third-party app support will rely on the existing CarPlay framework, rather than requiring developers to build apps specifically for the device. It remains unclear, though, whether this will extend to other CarPlay app categories, such as communication and AI assistants, or also be limited to media apps. We have reached out to Apple for clarification on how third-party app support will work, and will update this post if we hear back. Are you getting an Apple HomeView? Let us know in the comments. extraction.body: Apple today announced HomeView, a $299 smart home display with a 7-inch screen that lets users control connected accessories, make FaceTime calls, and enjoy music and video content. But what about third-party apps? Here’s what Apple says. Apple says the new HomeView smart home display is “designed for life at home,” with a wide range of features for managing connected accessories, staying organized, and enjoying entertainment. That includes everything from controlling smart home devices and checking calendars to watching videos, listening to music, and making FaceTime calls. However, one question Apple’s announcement didn’t fully answer is the extent to which HomeView will support third-party apps. According to Apple, in addition to a selection of Apple apps, including Music, Podcasts, and Safari, HomeView will also support “compatible third-party audio and video apps from your iPhone for a familiar experience across devices.” Interestingly, the fine print for this feature differs between Apple’s HomeView marketing page and the product’s press release. The press release , however, includes an additional detail (emphasis ours): Subscription may be required to access some content and services. Some applications are not available in all areas. Select apps require a paired and compatible iPhone nearby. Some of Apple’s own first-party apps will also be available from the iPhone, the company notes. That includes Audiobooks, Apple Music Classical, News, and TV. Apple has yet to detail how the iPhone proximity requirement will work, and whether developers of apps in supported categories will need to take any additional steps to support HomeView. Not trying to be the negative Nancy here but does this actually look like a useful product that will sell much outside of the apple customer that needs to get anything they put out? I know some have talked in the past about wanting something in the kitchen but what does this do that an iPad can't do for those needs? If this came out 15+ years ago, I could see it catching on for awhile before people realized they could get other devices to do what it does better. Apple is usually good with knowing their markets so I guess we'll see. This just feels like it's going against the direction of everything else. Most desktop computer users went to laptops, tablets, and phones already meaning having a static device and going mobile...or so I thought. According ot Wired , “a handful of third-party media apps like Spotify are available, and developers can bring over existing CarPlay apps.” Wired adds that “if your iPhone already has one of these CarPlay apps installed, it can automatically appear on the HomeView after setup.” So it looks like HomeView’s third-party app support will rely on the existing CarPlay framework, rather than requiring developers to build apps specifically for the device. It remains unclear, though, whether this will extend to other CarPlay app categories, such as communication and AI assistants, or also be limited to media apps. We have reached out to Apple for clarification on how third-party app support will work, and will update this post if we hear back. Are you getting an Apple HomeView? Let us know in the comments. extraction.body: Security researcher Dor Zvi and his team at the cybersecurity firm he cofounded, RedAccess, analyzed thousands of vibe-coded web applications created using the AI software development tools Lovable, Replit, Base44, and Netlify and found more than 5,000 of them that had virtually no security or authentication of any kind. Many of these web apps allowed anyone who merely finds their web URL to access the apps and their data. Around 40 percent of the apps exposed sensitive data, Zvi says, including medical information, financial data, corporate presentations, and strategy documents, as well as detailed logs of customer conversations with chatbots. “The end result is that organizations are actually leaking private data through vibe-coding applications,” says Zvi. “This is one of the biggest events ever where people are exposing corporate or other sensitive information to anyone in the world.” Zvi says RedAccess’ scouring for vulnerable web apps was surprisingly easy. Lovable, Replit, Base44, and Netlify all allow users to host their web apps on those AI companies' own domains, rather than the users’. So the researchers used straightforward Google and Bing searches for those AI companies' domains combined with other search terms to identify thousands of apps that had been vibe coded with the companies' tools. Of the 5,000 AI-coded apps that Zvi says were left publicly accessible to anyone who simply typed their URLs into a browser, he found close to 2,000 that, upon closer inspection, seemed to reveal private data: Screenshots of web apps he shared with WIRED—several of which WIRED verified were still online and exposed—showed what appeared to be a hospital's work assignments with the personally identifiable information of doctors, a company's detailed ad purchasing information, what appeared to be another firm's go-to-market strategy presentation, a retailer's full logs of its chatbot's conversations with customers, including the customers' full names and contact information, a shipping firm's cargo records, and assorted sales and financial records from a variety of other companies. In some cases, Zvi says, he found that the exposed apps would have allowed him to gain administrative privileges over systems and even remove other administrators. In the case of Lovable, Zvi says he also found numerous examples of phishing sites that impersonated major corporations, including Bank of America, Costco, FedEx, Trader Joe’s, and McDonald’s, that appeared to have been created with the AI coding tool and hosted on Lovable's domain. When WIRED asked the four AI coding companies about RedAccess’ findings, Netlify didn’t respond, but the three other companies pushed back on the researchers’ claims and protested that they hadn't shared enough of their findings or provided enough time for them to respond. (RedAccess says it reached out to the companies on Monday.) But they didn't deny that the web apps RedAccess found were left exposed. “From the limited information they shared, [RedAccess's] core claim appears to be that some users have published apps on the open web that should’ve been private,” Replit's CEO Amjad Masad wrote in a response post on X. “Replit allows users to choose whether apps are public or private. Public apps being accessible on the internet is expected behavior. Privacy settings can be changed at any time with a single click.” A spokesperson for Lovable responded in a statement that “Lovable takes reports of exposed data and phishing sites seriously, and we're actively working to obtain what we need to investigate. It's also worth noting that Lovable gives builders the tools to build securely, but how an app is configured is ultimately the creator's responsibility.” Blake Brodie, the head of public relations for Base44's parent company, Wix, wrote in a statement that “Base44 provides users with robust tools to configure their own applications' security, including access controls and visibility settings.” She added that “disabling those controls is a deliberate, straightforward action, any user can do it. Where applications were publicly accessible, that reflects a user configuration choice, not a platform vulnerability.” Brodie also noted that “it is trivially easy to fabricate applications that appear to contain real user data. Without a single verified example provided to us, we have no way to assess the validity of these claims.” RedAccess, for its part, disputed that it hadn't provided examples to Base44. Zvi notes that for a few dozen exposed web apps, it went so far as to contact the app's apparent owner, which confirmed that data had been exposed. RedAccess also shared with WIRED anonymized communications in several cases that showed Base44 users thanking the researchers for alerting them to exposed web apps, which were then secured or taken offline. Verifying whether real data has been exposed on any particular unsecured AI-coded web app can be tricky, says Joel Margolis, a security researcher who, along with a colleague, recently discovered that an AI chat toy had exposed 50,000 conversations the toy had with children on a website with virtually no security. Data in a vibe-coded web app might be a placeholder, he says, or the app might be just a proof of concept. Wix’s Brodie argued that two examples that WIRED shared with Base44 did appear to be test sites or have AI-generated data. For the web apps WIRED reviewed, we couldn't confirm that the personal or corporate data was as sensitive—or real—as it appeared to be. Margolis nonetheless says that the problem of AI-built web apps exposing data is very real. “Somebody from a marketing team wants to create a website. And unless you ask them to do it securely, they're not going to go out of their way to do that.” Zvi points out that the 5,000 exposed apps Red Access found were only those hosted on the AI coding tools' own domains, and that likely thousands more are hosted on users' own purchased domains. He compares the ongoing deluge of data exposures that are resulting from companies' unsecured AI-coded web apps to the epidemic of exposed data created by the security settings of Amazon S3 storage buckets in earlier years. Companies from Verizon to World Wrestling Entertainment accidentally exposed reams of sensitive data due to misconfigurations in their instance of Amazon's cloud storage service. AI web-app coding tools are now creating a wave of data exposures, the result of a similar combination of user error and lack of safeguards, Zvi says. Yet more fundamental than any particular security failing on the part of the AI coding companies, he argues, is simply that these tools allow a new class of people within organizations to create applications—often with little security awareness and outside the usual software development processes that companies use to vet applications before they're released. “Anyone from your company at any moment can generate an app, and this is not going through any development cycle or any security check,” Zvi says. “People can just start using it in production without asking anyone.

Of the 5,000 AI-coded apps that Zvi says were left publicly accessible to anyone who simply typed their URLs into a browser, he found close to 2,000 that, upon closer inspection, seemed to reveal private data: Screenshots of web apps he shared with WIRED—several of which WIRED verified were still online and exposed—showed what appeared to be a hospital's work assignments with the personally identifiable information of doctors, a company's detailed ad purchasing information, what appeared to be another firm's go-to-market strategy presentation, a retailer's full logs of its chatbot's conversations with customers, including the customers' full names and contact information, a shipping firm's cargo records, and assorted sales and financial records from a variety of other companies.
In some cases, Zvi says, he found that the exposed apps would have allowed him to gain administrative privileges over systems and even remove other administrators.

In the case of Lovable, Zvi says he also found numerous examples of phishing sites that impersonated major corporations, including Bank of America, Costco, FedEx, Trader Joe’s, and McDonald’s, that appeared to have been created with the AI coding tool and hosted on Lovable's domain.

When WIRED asked the four AI coding companies about RedAccess’ findings, Netlify didn’t respond, but the three other companies pushed back on the researchers’ claims and protested that they hadn't shared enough of their findings or provided enough time for them to respond. (RedAccess says it reached out to the companies on Monday.) But they didn't deny that the web apps RedAccess found were left exposed.

“From the limited information they shared, [RedAccess's] core claim appears to be that some users have published apps on the open web that should’ve been private,” Replit's CEO Amjad Masad wrote in a response post on X.
“Replit allows users to choose whether apps are public or private.
Public apps being accessible on the internet is expected behavior.

Privacy settings can be changed at any time with a single click.” A spokesperson for Lovable responded in a statement that “Lovable takes reports of exposed data and phishing sites seriously, and we're actively working to obtain what we need to investigate.

It's also worth noting that Lovable gives builders the tools to build securely, but how an app is configured is ultimately the creator's responsibility.” Blake Brodie, the head of public relations for Base44's parent company, Wix, wrote in a statement that “Base44 provides users with robust tools to configure their own applications' security, including access controls and visibility settings.” She added that “disabling those controls is a deliberate, straightforward action, any user can do it.

Where applications were publicly accessible, that reflects a user configuration choice, not a platform vulnerability.” Brodie also noted that “it is trivially easy to fabricate applications that appear to contain real user data.
Without a single verified example provided to us, we have no way to assess the validity of these claims.” RedAccess, for its part, disputed that it hadn't provided examples to Base44.
Zvi notes that for a few dozen exposed web apps, it went so far as to contact the app's apparent owner, which confirmed that data had been exposed.

RedAccess also shared with WIRED anonymized communications in several cases that showed Base44 users thanking the researchers for alerting them to exposed web apps, which were then secured or taken offline.

Verifying whether real data has been exposed on any particular unsecured AI-coded web app can be tricky, says Joel Margolis, a security researcher who, along with a colleague, recently discovered that an AI chat toy had exposed 50,000 conversations the toy had with children on a website with virtually no security.
Data in a vibe-coded web app might be a placeholder, he says, or the app might be just a proof of concept.
Wix’s Brodie argued that two examples that WIRED shared with Base44 did appear to be test sites or have AI-generated data.
For the web apps WIRED reviewed, we couldn't confirm that the personal or corporate data was as sensitive—or real—as it appeared to be.
Margolis nonetheless says that the problem of AI-built web apps exposing data is very real.
“Somebody from a marketing team wants to create a website.

And unless you ask them to do it securely, they're not going to go out of their way to do that.” Zvi points out that the 5,000 exposed apps Red Access found were only those hosted on the AI coding tools' own domains, and that likely thousands more are hosted on users' own purchased domains.

He compares the ongoing deluge of data exposures that are resulting from companies' unsecured AI-coded web apps to the epidemic of exposed data created by the security settings of Amazon S3 storage buckets in earlier years.
Companies from Verizon to World Wrestling Entertainment accidentally exposed reams of sensitive data due to misconfigurations in their instance of Amazon's cloud storage service.
AI web-app coding tools are now creating a wave of data exposures, the result of a similar combination of user error and lack of safeguards, Zvi says.

Yet more fundamental than any particular security failing on the part of the AI coding companies, he argues, is simply that these tools allow a new class of people within organizations to create applications—often with little security awareness and outside the usual software development processes that companies use to vet applications before they're released.
“Anyone from your company at any moment can generate an app, and this is not going through any development cycle or any security check,” Zvi says.
“People can just start using it in production without asking anyone.

Are you tired of ad overload in free, single-task apps? Or, can you not find an app that fits a weirdly specific need? Now you can make custom apps for your own Android phone, even if you have zero coding experience. One Tuesday, Google announced that anyone with a standard Google account can build personal apps in Google AI Studio. These apps will run on your own device, launched from a private part of Google Play, and won’t be included in the public Play Store. Also: ‘What’s your AI stack?’ The new job interview question you need to answer You’ll be able to share your apps with close family and friends in the coming months, but you don’t have to. If you do share an app you create and it takes off, Google will provide a “pipeline to graduate into a professional developer account,” meaning you’ll be able to share your app globally via the Play Store. To get started, access the tool in Google AI Studio . There is an app creator in AI Studio, but that’s intended for professional developer accounts and requires USB debugging connected to a PC. This new tool works with that same creator, but it lets you install your app on a personal device with a single click and later directly share it instead of utilizing a public Play Store listing. In the tool, you describe what you want in a prompt, and AI does the rest. While the app is under creation, you’ll see options to add features you might have missed. You can make light edits once the app is complete, or you can completely scrap it and start again. There’s no charge to experiment and build an app. Custom Android apps make app development a much more personal and potentially user-friendly experience. It could be a fantastic option for replacing apps on your phone that you only use for a single thing – like a habit tracker, a calculator or converter, or a specific counter or timer. The ability to make an app with AI isn’t new, but the big selling point here is that you can make an app completely for yourself . Also: I used a free, open-source AI tool to build a working app – in two days My wife had surgery recently, and part of her recovery involves an array of specifically timed medicines, supplements, and liquids. She downloaded a simple tracker app to stay on top of things, but the app was loaded with ads to the point it was too frustrating to use. A monthly subscription was offered to nix the ads, but she didn’t want to pay for an app that would only be used for a few months. Searching for similar apps yielded similar results. With Google’s new system, it seems like it would be simple to make a custom app that avoids both the ads and the fees. And even better, you can tailor this app specifically to what you need. Perhaps the best part about this system is that an app you make doesn’t have to be commercially viable, and it doesn’t even have to be an app that anyone else needs. It just has to work for you . sources.title: Google wants to host your personal vibe-coded apps in the Play Store
passages: There won’t be any tedious downloading of APK files or tinkering with a developer console—you’ll be able to send apps to the Play Store right from AI Studio.
This is available only to you by default, providing an easy way to install and manage the apps via Google’s system.

The previously released Ask Play feature is expanding to offer more AI-powered discovery options in Google’s app store, and Google is also using AI to build a recommendation engine called Game Finder.
Despite its slow progress in coding-focused AI models lately, Google is continuing to push this as a core feature of its products.
This is not the same as publishing an app as a developer, but that could be the end result.
Google says you can share these apps with “a small group” of friends and family.
Google rolled out Ask Play in 2025 as a small chatbot interface on Play Store listings.
It lets you ask questions about an app or game, either by typing it in manually or choosing from a list of suggested queries.
You ask the robot questions, and it generates recommendations that can include detailed comparison charts.
Gemini will roll out a similar capability soon.
The private-to-public app migration option will be available in the coming months.
You can tune your DNA profile by rating the games you’ve played, which supposedly leads to more accurate recommendations.
There will be game playlists to peruse, along with various contextual lists like relaxing, trending titles, and more specific lists based on mechanics you’ve seen in previous games.
Game Finder and Gamer DNA are rolling out in the US today, with other markets following “soon.”
Google plans to help turn those personal AI-generated apps into wide releases.
Google’s other AI discovery announcement focuses on games.
It builds a profile called Gamer DNA and matches you with players who have similar DNA.

extraction.body: Google plans to help turn those personal AI-generated apps into wide releases. Google has already added a few AI features to the Play Store, but a lot more are coming . The previously released Ask Play feature is expanding to offer more AI-powered discovery options in Google’s app store, and Google is also using AI to build a recommendation engine called Game Finder. For people who have embraced AI to build their own apps, the Play Store will soon offer a way to privately host and share those creations. Google rolled out Ask Play in 2025 as a small chatbot interface on Play Store listings. It lets you ask questions about an app or game, either by typing it in manually or choosing from a list of suggested queries. Starting today, Ask Play is expanding into a more general way to search for apps and games. You ask the robot questions, and it generates recommendations that can include detailed comparison charts. Gemini will roll out a similar capability soon. Google’s other AI discovery announcement focuses on games. The new Game Finder feature leans on all the usage data Google’s app platform has hoovered up over the years, featuring insights into the way 1.2 billion people play games on Android. It builds a profile called Gamer DNA and matches you with players who have similar DNA. You can tune your DNA profile by rating the games you’ve played, which supposedly leads to more accurate recommendations. There will be game playlists to peruse, along with various contextual lists like relaxing, trending titles, and more specific lists based on mechanics you’ve seen in previous games. Game Finder also lets you add or remove tags to further adjust the games Google’s AI suggests. Google says you’ll eventually be able to prompt Game Finder with fairly specific game preferences, but it’s unclear how much customization will be available at launch. Game Finder and Gamer DNA are rolling out in the US today, with other markets following “soon.” Despite its slow progress in coding-focused AI models lately, Google is continuing to push this as a core feature of its products. Anyone who has been tinkering with vibe-coded apps in AI Studio will soon have a direct pipe into the Play Store. This is not the same as publishing an app as a developer, but that could be the end result. There won’t be any tedious downloading of APK files or tinkering with a developer console—you’ll be able to send apps to the Play Store right from AI Studio. Adding a vibe coded app to the Play Store creates a “Personal Library” accessible from the app store client on your device. This is available only to you by default, providing an easy way to install and manage the apps via Google’s system. Google says you can share these apps with “a small group” of friends and family. Google has not decided how many people count as a small group yet, but this type of distribution doesn’t require a developer account. If you want to share beyond that, Google plans to have an onboarding process to set you up with a developer profile to publish your vibe coded apps. If you do this, you’ll be subject to the same app review guidelines as developers who come into Google Play in the traditional way. Private apps are not reviewed by Google. Private vibe-coded apps in the Play Store will begin rolling out today in the US and select other markets. The private-to-public app migration option will be available in the coming months. passages: I found an app called Hotkeys that seemed to do what I wanted, but it left the App Store quite a while ago, presumably because it was designed for Intel-based hardware. (Apple is ending support for such apps with macOS 28.) You May Also Like But now that Golden Gate has deeper Apple Intelligence tools, I decided to use Claude Code and Xcode to vibe code a modern, intuitive, and unobtrusive hotkey app called KeyRun.
You can tell Claude not to waste tokens by complimenting you, but even an AI agent’s praise is good to have, so I didn't.

extraction.body: I've always wanted a straightforward way to launch apps, open documents in their default apps, or bring up folders on macOS via hotkeys. To do the same in macOS, you either have to build a multistep process via the Shortcuts app or download a third-party utility such as FastScripts 3 , HomeRow , Karabiner-Elements , Keyboard Maestro , or Raycast . These apps and others that I've tried work, but they are either unnecessarily complex or cost more than I want to spend. I found an app called Hotkeys that seemed to do what I wanted, but it left the App Store quite a while ago, presumably because it was designed for Intel-based hardware. (Apple is ending support for such apps with macOS 28.) You May Also Like But now that Golden Gate has deeper Apple Intelligence tools, I decided to use Claude Code and Xcode to vibe code a modern, intuitive, and unobtrusive hotkey app called KeyRun. And, of course, I made it free for anyone to download from the Mac App Store. Setting Up the AI Workbench in macOS Golden Gate Apple’s Xcode programming app already had AI integrations in macOS Sequoia , but the connections are tighter in the Golden Gate beta. For one, your conversations now take place in the main Xcode window rather than in a sidebar. Installing Claude (Credit: Apple/PCMag) To get started, you’ll need a Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini chatbot account. Then, in Xcode, simply go to Settings > Intelligence and click Get next to the agent you want to install. I chose Claude and got right into prompting . Prompting KeyRun to Life—and Bypassing Mac's Permissions Trap I began by asking Claude, “Can you create a simple, intuitive macOS app that assigns hotkeys to applications, so that I can submit it to the App Store? I want the app to create a hotkey for any app that I either drag into the app’s window or choose from a list of files.” Claude complied, and in a few seconds, it coded an app that matched my specifications. I was able to view the actual code by opening its files from the Xcode sidebar. I then asked Claude to rewrite the app so that it wouldn’t create hotkeys that macOS already uses , such as Cmd-Q (quit the current app) or Cmd-S (save the current document). It agreed to this and subsequently made the app check any new shortcuts against the list of system-wide hotkeys that macOS maintains in the background. Coding with Claude (Credit: Apple/PCMag) But then I hit a complication. When I tried to use a hotkey I had created, macOS told me I needed to grant it Accessibility permission in the System Settings app. I didn’t want prospective users to deal with this annoyance, so I asked Claude if a workaround was possible. Claude immediately solved the problem by rewriting the app’s hotkey mechanism to use Apple’s ancient Carbon framework instead of the modern AppKit’s global event monitor. Apple officially states that Carbon, in general, is deprecated, but it never explicitly got rid of the Carbon hotkey mechanism and has even updated it for 64-bit macOS environments. Almost all existing hotkey apps use this mechanism, so it's not likely to go away anytime soon. At this point, Claude suggested that we save the project and give it a name. Claude, sounding like a restaurant waiter who says “Excellent Choice!” no matter what you choose from the menu, told me it was an excellent name. You can tell Claude not to waste tokens by complimenting you, but even an AI agent’s praise is good to have, so I didn't. Then, I got ambitious and asked Claude to add a feature that could open documents, not only apps, from a hotkey. Claude did exactly that, adding the detail that it would add only those documents that normally open in a default app when you double-click on them. I pushed things further by asking for an option to open folders with hotkeys. Every time Claude added a feature, I thought of another. I also had Claude build a “save” feature that saves a set of keyboard shortcuts to a file, so that I could copy the file to another system and use the same hotkeys. The last thing I did was add an option to launch KeyRun automatically upon startup. passages: I've always wanted a straightforward way to launch apps, open documents in their default apps, or bring up folders on macOS via hotkeys.

To do the same in macOS, you either have to build a multistep process via the Shortcuts app or download a third-party utility such as FastScripts 3 , HomeRow , Karabiner-Elements , Keyboard Maestro , or Raycast .
These apps and others that I've tried work, but they are either unnecessarily complex or cost more than I want to spend.

I found an app called Hotkeys that seemed to do what I wanted, but it left the App Store quite a while ago, presumably because it was designed for Intel-based hardware. (Apple is ending support for such apps with macOS 28.) You May Also Like But now that Golden Gate has deeper Apple Intelligence tools, I decided to use Claude Code and Xcode to vibe code a modern, intuitive, and unobtrusive hotkey app called KeyRun.
And, of course, I made it free for anyone to download from the Mac App Store.
Setting Up the AI Workbench in macOS Golden Gate Apple’s Xcode programming app already had AI integrations in macOS Sequoia , but the connections are tighter in the Golden Gate beta.
For one, your conversations now take place in the main Xcode window rather than in a sidebar.
Installing Claude (Credit: Apple/PCMag) To get started, you’ll need a Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini chatbot account.
Then, in Xcode, simply go to Settings > Intelligence and click Get next to the agent you want to install.
I chose Claude and got right into prompting .

Prompting KeyRun to Life—and Bypassing Mac's Permissions Trap I began by asking Claude, “Can you create a simple, intuitive macOS app that assigns hotkeys to applications, so that I can submit it to the App Store?

I want the app to create a hotkey for any app that I either drag into the app’s window or choose from a list of files.” Claude complied, and in a few seconds, it coded an app that matched my specifications.
I was able to view the actual code by opening its files from the Xcode sidebar.
I then asked Claude to rewrite the app so that it wouldn’t create hotkeys that macOS already uses , such as Cmd-Q (quit the current app) or Cmd-S (save the current document).
It agreed to this and subsequently made the app check any new shortcuts against the list of system-wide hotkeys that macOS maintains in the background.

When I tried to use a hotkey I had created, macOS told me I needed to grant it Accessibility permission in the System Settings app.
I didn’t want prospective users to deal with this annoyance, so I asked Claude if a workaround was possible.
Claude immediately solved the problem by rewriting the app’s hotkey mechanism to use Apple’s ancient Carbon framework instead of the modern AppKit’s global event monitor.
Apple officially states that Carbon, in general, is deprecated, but it never explicitly got rid of the Carbon hotkey mechanism and has even updated it for 64-bit macOS environments.
Almost all existing hotkey apps use this mechanism, so it's not likely to go away anytime soon.
At this point, Claude suggested that we save the project and give it a name.
Claude, sounding like a restaurant waiter who says “Excellent Choice!” no matter what you choose from the menu, told me it was an excellent name.
You can tell Claude not to waste tokens by complimenting you, but even an AI agent’s praise is good to have, so I didn't.
Then, I got ambitious and asked Claude to add a feature that could open documents, not only apps, from a hotkey.

Finally, I asked Claude to create a hotkey for KeyRun itself.

extraction.body: Security researcher Dor Zvi and his team at the cybersecurity firm he cofounded, RedAccess, analyzed thousands of vibe-coded web applications created using the AI software development tools Lovable, Replit, Base44, and Netlify and found more than 5,000 of them that had virtually no security or authentication of any kind. Many of these web apps allowed anyone who merely finds their web URL to access the apps and their data. Around 40 percent of the apps exposed sensitive data, Zvi says, including medical information, financial data, corporate presentations, and strategy documents, as well as detailed logs of customer conversations with chatbots. “The end result is that organizations are actually leaking private data through vibe-coding applications,” says Zvi. “This is one of the biggest events ever where people are exposing corporate or other sensitive information to anyone in the world.” Zvi says RedAccess’ scouring for vulnerable web apps was surprisingly easy. Lovable, Replit, Base44, and Netlify all allow users to host their web apps on those AI companies' own domains, rather than the users’. So the researchers used straightforward Google and Bing searches for those AI companies' domains combined with other search terms to identify thousands of apps that had been vibe coded with the companies' tools. Of the 5,000 AI-coded apps that Zvi says were left publicly accessible to anyone who simply typed their URLs into a browser, he found close to 2,000 that, upon closer inspection, seemed to reveal private data: Screenshots of web apps he shared with WIRED—several of which WIRED verified were still online and exposed—showed what appeared to be a hospital's work assignments with the personally identifiable information of doctors, a company's detailed ad purchasing information, what appeared to be another firm's go-to-market strategy presentation, a retailer's full logs of its chatbot's conversations with customers, including the customers' full names and contact information, a shipping firm's cargo records, and assorted sales and financial records from a variety of other companies. In some cases, Zvi says, he found that the exposed apps would have allowed him to gain administrative privileges over systems and even remove other administrators. In the case of Lovable, Zvi says he also found numerous examples of phishing sites that impersonated major corporations, including Bank of America, Costco, FedEx, Trader Joe’s, and McDonald’s, that appeared to have been created with the AI coding tool and hosted on Lovable's domain. When WIRED asked the four AI coding companies about RedAccess’ findings, Netlify didn’t respond, but the three other companies pushed back on the researchers’ claims and protested that they hadn't shared enough of their findings or provided enough time for them to respond. (RedAccess says it reached out to the companies on Monday.) But they didn't deny that the web apps RedAccess found were left exposed. “From the limited information they shared, [RedAccess's] core claim appears to be that some users have published apps on the open web that should’ve been private,” Replit's CEO Amjad Masad wrote in a response post on X. “Replit allows users to choose whether apps are public or private. Public apps being accessible on the internet is expected behavior. Privacy settings can be changed at any time with a single click.” A spokesperson for Lovable responded in a statement that “Lovable takes reports of exposed data and phishing sites seriously, and we're actively working to obtain what we need to investigate. It's also worth noting that Lovable gives builders the tools to build securely, but how an app is configured is ultimately the creator's responsibility.” Blake Brodie, the head of public relations for Base44's parent company, Wix, wrote in a statement that “Base44 provides users with robust tools to configure their own applications' security, including access controls and visibility settings.” She added that “disabling those controls is a deliberate, straightforward action, any user can do it. Where applications were publicly accessible, that reflects a user configuration choice, not a platform vulnerability.” Brodie also noted that “it is trivially easy to fabricate applications that appear to contain real user data. Without a single verified example provided to us, we have no way to assess the validity of these claims.” RedAccess, for its part, disputed that it hadn't provided examples to Base44. Zvi notes that for a few dozen exposed web apps, it went so far as to contact the app's apparent owner, which confirmed that data had been exposed. RedAccess also shared with WIRED anonymized communications in several cases that showed Base44 users thanking the researchers for alerting them to exposed web apps, which were then secured or taken offline. Verifying whether real data has been exposed on any particular unsecured AI-coded web app can be tricky, says Joel Margolis, a security researcher who, along with a colleague, recently discovered that an AI chat toy had exposed 50,000 conversations the toy had with children on a website with virtually no security. Data in a vibe-coded web app might be a placeholder, he says, or the app might be just a proof of concept. Wix’s Brodie argued that two examples that WIRED shared with Base44 did appear to be test sites or have AI-generated data. For the web apps WIRED reviewed, we couldn't confirm that the personal or corporate data was as sensitive—or real—as it appeared to be. Margolis nonetheless says that the problem of AI-built web apps exposing data is very real. “Somebody from a marketing team wants to create a website. And unless you ask them to do it securely, they're not going to go out of their way to do that.” Zvi points out that the 5,000 exposed apps Red Access found were only those hosted on the AI coding tools' own domains, and that likely thousands more are hosted on users' own purchased domains. He compares the ongoing deluge of data exposures that are resulting from companies' unsecured AI-coded web apps to the epidemic of exposed data created by the security settings of Amazon S3 storage buckets in earlier years. Companies from Verizon to World Wrestling Entertainment accidentally exposed reams of sensitive data due to misconfigurations in their instance of Amazon's cloud storage service. AI web-app coding tools are now creating a wave of data exposures, the result of a similar combination of user error and lack of safeguards, Zvi says. Yet more fundamental than any particular security failing on the part of the AI coding companies, he argues, is simply that these tools allow a new class of people within organizations to create applications—often with little security awareness and outside the usual software development processes that companies use to vet applications before they're released. “Anyone from your company at any moment can generate an app, and this is not going through any development cycle or any security check,” Zvi says. “People can just start using it in production without asking anyone.

Are you tired of ad overload in free, single-task apps? Or, can you not find an app that fits a weirdly specific need? Now you can make custom apps for your own Android phone, even if you have zero coding experience. One Tuesday, Google announced that anyone with a standard Google account can build personal apps in Google AI Studio. These apps will run on your own device, launched from a private part of Google Play, and won’t be included in the public Play Store. Also: ‘What’s your AI stack?’ The new job interview question you need to answer You’ll be able to share your apps with close family and friends in the coming months, but you don’t have to. If you do share an app you create and it takes off, Google will provide a “pipeline to graduate into a professional developer account,” meaning you’ll be able to share your app globally via the Play Store. To get started, access the tool in Google AI Studio . There is an app creator in AI Studio, but that’s intended for professional developer accounts and requires USB debugging connected to a PC. This new tool works with that same creator, but it lets you install your app on a personal device with a single click and later directly share it instead of utilizing a public Play Store listing. In the tool, you describe what you want in a prompt, and AI does the rest. While the app is under creation, you’ll see options to add features you might have missed. You can make light edits once the app is complete, or you can completely scrap it and start again. There’s no charge to experiment and build an app. Custom Android apps make app development a much more personal and potentially user-friendly experience. It could be a fantastic option for replacing apps on your phone that you only use for a single thing – like a habit tracker, a calculator or converter, or a specific counter or timer. The ability to make an app with AI isn’t new, but the big selling point here is that you can make an app completely for yourself . Also: I used a free, open-source AI tool to build a working app – in two days My wife had surgery recently, and part of her recovery involves an array of specifically timed medicines, supplements, and liquids. She downloaded a simple tracker app to stay on top of things, but the app was loaded with ads to the point it was too frustrating to use. A monthly subscription was offered to nix the ads, but she didn’t want to pay for an app that would only be used for a few months. Searching for similar apps yielded similar results. With Google’s new system, it seems like it would be simple to make a custom app that avoids both the ads and the fees. And even better, you can tailor this app specifically to what you need. Perhaps the best part about this system is that an app you make doesn’t have to be commercially viable, and it doesn’t even have to be an app that anyone else needs. It just has to work for you . sources.title: Google wants to host your personal vibe-coded apps in the Play Store
passages: There won’t be any tedious downloading of APK files or tinkering with a developer console—you’ll be able to send apps to the Play Store right from AI Studio.
This is available only to you by default, providing an easy way to install and manage the apps via Google’s system.

The previously released Ask Play feature is expanding to offer more AI-powered discovery options in Google’s app store, and Google is also using AI to build a recommendation engine called Game Finder.
Despite its slow progress in coding-focused AI models lately, Google is continuing to push this as a core feature of its products.
This is not the same as publishing an app as a developer, but that could be the end result.
Google says you can share these apps with “a small group” of friends and family.
Google rolled out Ask Play in 2025 as a small chatbot interface on Play Store listings.
It lets you ask questions about an app or game, either by typing it in manually or choosing from a list of suggested queries.
You ask the robot questions, and it generates recommendations that can include detailed comparison charts.
Gemini will roll out a similar capability soon.
The private-to-public app migration option will be available in the coming months.
You can tune your DNA profile by rating the games you’ve played, which supposedly leads to more accurate recommendations.
There will be game playlists to peruse, along with various contextual lists like relaxing, trending titles, and more specific lists based on mechanics you’ve seen in previous games.
Game Finder and Gamer DNA are rolling out in the US today, with other markets following “soon.”
Google plans to help turn those personal AI-generated apps into wide releases.
Google’s other AI discovery announcement focuses on games.
It builds a profile called Gamer DNA and matches you with players who have similar DNA.

extraction.body: Google plans to help turn those personal AI-generated apps into wide releases. Google has already added a few AI features to the Play Store, but a lot more are coming . The previously released Ask Play feature is expanding to offer more AI-powered discovery options in Google’s app store, and Google is also using AI to build a recommendation engine called Game Finder. For people who have embraced AI to build their own apps, the Play Store will soon offer a way to privately host and share those creations. Google rolled out Ask Play in 2025 as a small chatbot interface on Play Store listings. It lets you ask questions about an app or game, either by typing it in manually or choosing from a list of suggested queries. Starting today, Ask Play is expanding into a more general way to search for apps and games. You ask the robot questions, and it generates recommendations that can include detailed comparison charts. Gemini will roll out a similar capability soon. Google’s other AI discovery announcement focuses on games. The new Game Finder feature leans on all the usage data Google’s app platform has hoovered up over the years, featuring insights into the way 1.2 billion people play games on Android. It builds a profile called Gamer DNA and matches you with players who have similar DNA. You can tune your DNA profile by rating the games you’ve played, which supposedly leads to more accurate recommendations. There will be game playlists to peruse, along with various contextual lists like relaxing, trending titles, and more specific lists based on mechanics you’ve seen in previous games. Game Finder also lets you add or remove tags to further adjust the games Google’s AI suggests. Google says you’ll eventually be able to prompt Game Finder with fairly specific game preferences, but it’s unclear how much customization will be available at launch. Game Finder and Gamer DNA are rolling out in the US today, with other markets following “soon.” Despite its slow progress in coding-focused AI models lately, Google is continuing to push this as a core feature of its products. Anyone who has been tinkering with vibe-coded apps in AI Studio will soon have a direct pipe into the Play Store. This is not the same as publishing an app as a developer, but that could be the end result. There won’t be any tedious downloading of APK files or tinkering with a developer console—you’ll be able to send apps to the Play Store right from AI Studio. Adding a vibe coded app to the Play Store creates a “Personal Library” accessible from the app store client on your device. This is available only to you by default, providing an easy way to install and manage the apps via Google’s system. Google says you can share these apps with “a small group” of friends and family. Google has not decided how many people count as a small group yet, but this type of distribution doesn’t require a developer account. If you want to share beyond that, Google plans to have an onboarding process to set you up with a developer profile to publish your vibe coded apps. If you do this, you’ll be subject to the same app review guidelines as developers who come into Google Play in the traditional way. Private apps are not reviewed by Google. Private vibe-coded apps in the Play Store will begin rolling out today in the US and select other markets. The private-to-public app migration option will be available in the coming months. extraction.body: I've always wanted a straightforward way to launch apps, open documents in their default apps, or bring up folders on macOS via hotkeys. To do the same in macOS, you either have to build a multistep process via the Shortcuts app or download a third-party utility such as FastScripts 3 , HomeRow , Karabiner-Elements , Keyboard Maestro , or Raycast . These apps and others that I've tried work, but they are either unnecessarily complex or cost more than I want to spend. I found an app called Hotkeys that seemed to do what I wanted, but it left the App Store quite a while ago, presumably because it was designed for Intel-based hardware. (Apple is ending support for such apps with macOS 28.) You May Also Like But now that Golden Gate has deeper Apple Intelligence tools, I decided to use Claude Code and Xcode to vibe code a modern, intuitive, and unobtrusive hotkey app called KeyRun. And, of course, I made it free for anyone to download from the Mac App Store. Setting Up the AI Workbench in macOS Golden Gate Apple’s Xcode programming app already had AI integrations in macOS Sequoia , but the connections are tighter in the Golden Gate beta. For one, your conversations now take place in the main Xcode window rather than in a sidebar. Installing Claude (Credit: Apple/PCMag) To get started, you’ll need a Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini chatbot account. Then, in Xcode, simply go to Settings > Intelligence and click Get next to the agent you want to install. I chose Claude and got right into prompting . Prompting KeyRun to Life—and Bypassing Mac's Permissions Trap I began by asking Claude, “Can you create a simple, intuitive macOS app that assigns hotkeys to applications, so that I can submit it to the App Store? I want the app to create a hotkey for any app that I either drag into the app’s window or choose from a list of files.” Claude complied, and in a few seconds, it coded an app that matched my specifications. I was able to view the actual code by opening its files from the Xcode sidebar. I then asked Claude to rewrite the app so that it wouldn’t create hotkeys that macOS already uses , such as Cmd-Q (quit the current app) or Cmd-S (save the current document). It agreed to this and subsequently made the app check any new shortcuts against the list of system-wide hotkeys that macOS maintains in the background. Coding with Claude (Credit: Apple/PCMag) But then I hit a complication. When I tried to use a hotkey I had created, macOS told me I needed to grant it Accessibility permission in the System Settings app. I didn’t want prospective users to deal with this annoyance, so I asked Claude if a workaround was possible. Claude immediately solved the problem by rewriting the app’s hotkey mechanism to use Apple’s ancient Carbon framework instead of the modern AppKit’s global event monitor. Apple officially states that Carbon, in general, is deprecated, but it never explicitly got rid of the Carbon hotkey mechanism and has even updated it for 64-bit macOS environments. Almost all existing hotkey apps use this mechanism, so it's not likely to go away anytime soon. At this point, Claude suggested that we save the project and give it a name. Claude, sounding like a restaurant waiter who says “Excellent Choice!” no matter what you choose from the menu, told me it was an excellent name. You can tell Claude not to waste tokens by complimenting you, but even an AI agent’s praise is good to have, so I didn't. Then, I got ambitious and asked Claude to add a feature that could open documents, not only apps, from a hotkey. Claude did exactly that, adding the detail that it would add only those documents that normally open in a default app when you double-click on them. I pushed things further by asking for an option to open folders with hotkeys. Every time Claude added a feature, I thought of another. I also had Claude build a “save” feature that saves a set of keyboard shortcuts to a file, so that I could copy the file to another system and use the same hotkeys. After that, I had Claude add profiles so I could use a different set of hotkeys when working on documents and editing images. Finally, I asked Claude to create a hotkey for KeyRun itself. KeyRun app interface (Credit: Ed Mendelson/PCMag) At every stage, Claude and I consulted on which keyboard shortcuts to use in the app’s menus for each new feature. Claude suggested that the app should automatically delete the hotkey assignment if it couldn’t find the app or document associated with it, but I reminded Claude that the user might decide to bring back the app or document, and that the user should be able to decide whether to keep or delete an obsolete hotkey assignment—and Claude agreed. The last thing I did was add an option to launch KeyRun automatically upon startup. Surviving the App Store Review: Beta Bugs and Rejections When the app seemed complete, I asked Claude to guide me through submitting it to the Mac App Store. Of course, if you want to create an app just for personal needs, you can skip these steps.

facts.text: So the researchers used straightforward Google and Bing searches for those AI companies' domains combined with other search terms to identify thousands of apps that had been vibe coded with the companies' tools.

“From the limited information they shared, [RedAccess's] core claim appears to be that some users have published apps on the open web that should’ve been private,” Replit's CEO Amjad Masad wrote in a response post on X.

And unless you ask them to do it securely, they're not going to go out of their way to do that.” Zvi points out that the 5,000 exposed apps Red Access found were only those hosted on the AI coding tools' own domains, and that likely thousands more are hosted on users' own purchased domains.

Around 40 percent of the apps exposed sensitive data, Zvi says, including medical information, financial data, corporate presentations, and strategy documents, as well as detailed logs of customer conversations with chatbots.
Data in a vibe-coded web app might be a placeholder, he says, or the app might be just a proof of concept.
For the web apps WIRED reviewed, we couldn't confirm that the personal or corporate data was as sensitive—or real—as it appeared to be.

He compares the ongoing deluge of data exposures that are resulting from companies' unsecured AI-coded web apps to the epidemic of exposed data created by the security settings of Amazon S3 storage buckets in earlier years.
Are you tired of ad overload in free, single-task apps?
Or, can you not find an app that fits a weirdly specific need?
Now you can make custom apps for your own Android phone, even if you have zero coding experience.
One Tuesday, Google announced that anyone with a standard Google account can build personal apps in Google AI Studio.
These apps will run on your own device, launched from a private part of Google Play, and won’t be included in the public Play Store.
You’ll be able to share your apps with close family and friends in the coming months, but you don’t have to.
Custom Android apps make app development a much more personal and potentially user-friendly experience.

This is available only to you by default, providing an easy way to install and manage the apps via Google’s system.
