Apple this summer upgraded Siri’s capabilities with assistance from Google but analysts said it is unclear whether its AI assistant is competitive enough to lure consumers to a crowded connected home device space.

The device features a 7-inch screen — which Apple said is to make it fit into a home without being too imposing — similar to Apple’s “sunflower” iMac from the 2000s. And while it features a menu of square app icons like an iPhone or iPad that change depending on which user is recognized, Apple showed it being used more often via voice with its Siri AI assistant.
The launches also coincide with growing worries that connected devices, including refrigerators and smart TVs, could be vulnerable to hackers.

Apple accompanied the HomeView launch with updates to its HomePod smart speaker and Apple TV devices. It also introduced a range of accessories, including doorbells, cameras and thermostats, made by LG and Schneider Electric and designed with help from Apple.

Apple’s work with LG and Schneider Electric to sell a suite of products alongside the HomeView was meant to make it easier to add smart home products to a household. Kaiann Drance, Apple’s vice president of product marketing for home products, said the devices can be added with a single tap, similar to Apple’s first-party devices such as AirPods.
“For people who haven’t experienced the Home ecosystem or haven’t gone further than maybe a product here or there, I think this is a great opportunity to look,” Drance told Reuters in an interview.

Ben Wood, chief analyst and chief marketing officer for CCS Insight, said that at first glance Apple’s partnership with the two outside firms looked like a break with its usual practice of fully controlling its hardware.

“However, looking closely, it appears like there has been very deep collaboration between Apple and these partners to ensure the design, engineering and experience closely match what users would expect from Apple,” he said.

During a video demonstrating the device, Apple showed the HomeView, which is meant to hang on walls or perch on tabletops, and its Siri virtual assistant juggling voice requests from multiple members of a family at the same time.
To pull in private data from messages and calendars, the HomeView relies on a user having an iPhone that’s been recently unlocked and connected to the same home network.
The HomeView device will not be sold in the European Union, because Siri AI remains unavailable there due to EU regulations, Apple said.

Analysts said two major hurdles for Apple were making its devices work with a variety of third-party gadgets and the limited ability of Siri to give useful answers.
“Apple has the brand, technology and loyal customers to make a serious impact, but it is playing catch-up with rivals that have a far stronger presence,” Pescatore said.

Fragmentation among various companies’ “smart” home products and the difficulty of connecting them has proved a hurdle to the market’s growth although there is hope that AI-enabled devices from Apple, Google and Amazon could make integration more seamless.

“Most smart speakers and hubs in homes today are low-cost devices that can’t run AI at the edge, so they are ripe for replacement,” said Mohit Agrawal, Research Director at Counterpoint. “Amazon and Google have only just begun refreshing their hardware for Alexa+ and Gemini, so the upgrade cycle is wide open, and Apple wants to win it.”
Apple’s $299 price for HomeView is above Amazon’s Echo Show 8 at $199.99 and Google’s Nest Hub at $99.99, as it seeks a bigger role in connected homes.

"Advances in AI should finally make a difference, but Apple still needs to show whether it can simplify connectivity and work with devices across the wider smart home market rather than restricting users to its own ecosystem," O'Donnell said.

Greater artificial intelligence functionality could make voice-controlled home management more useful, particularly when coordinating several connected devices.

sources.title: Where Tom Tiffany and David Crowley stand on Wisconsin data centers - Wausau Pilot & Review
passages: MADISON – The two major candidates running to be Wisconsin’s next governor are battling to gain the upper hand on an emerging issue that neither political party owns yet: data centers.
The next governor will undoubtedly reckon with the construction boom in the Badger State of the increasingly controversial factories of artificial intelligence.

As more massive technology centers are stood up across the state, Wisconsin voters of all political stripes are growing more opposed to them, with nearly 80% of voters saying in a recent statewide poll that the costs of building data centers outweigh the benefits.
“There should be full transparency, and we will ban NDAs that keep communities in the dark,” Tiffany told the Journal Sentinel.

Both candidates also said they want the companies that build the data centers to pay for their own energy. “Any costs created by data centers must be paid by the facilities themselves, not passed on to Wisconsin families and businesses through higher utility bills, and they must adhere to the Ratepayer Protection Pledge and bring their own energy,” Tiffany said, referring to an order issued by President Donald Trump on data center regulation.
Published content is property of Wausau Pilot and Review.

extraction.body: Gorman, who has been on the Rock County Board of Supervisors since 2024, began organizing with citizens across the county who feared that the project would raise utility bills, diminish air quality, and drain the county’s groundwater, joining a growing nationwide backlash against data centers. “I’ve never seen engagement like this on any normal development issue,” Gorman said. “People don’t like that they didn’t have a vote on whether social media could take over our society. And now people see A.I. getting ready to take things over and potentially upset lives, upset society, upset jobs, and they want the ability to have a say in that.” Local residents helped set up informal community meetings to discuss the data center at the public library, and opposition kept building. “I won very conservative parts of the town of Beloit that I had previously lost, purely on the data-center issue,” he told me. “You can knock seven doors and hear seven different reasons why people don’t want this.” A recent Gallup poll found that more than seventy per cent of Americans oppose data centers in their area. And, during the past several weeks, data centers have become increasingly toxic in midterm elections across the country. Opposition has become particularly central to contests in Rust Belt states, such as Republican-trending Ohio, where anti-data-center policies have appeared to boost the campaigns of the Democrats Amy Acton, who is running for governor, and Sherrod Brown, who is running for Senate. Brown’s opponent is the incumbent Jon Husted, who previously, as lieutenant governor, helped usher in an explosion of data centers in the state, many of which were developed after Ohio offered them lucrative tax breaks. Brown’s ability to hammer Husted on this issue is alarming Republican operatives, who see a Husted victory as crucial to holding a majority in the Senate. This month, Axios released a private memo from the National Republican Senatorial Committee warning that data centers have become an “anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.” Other politicians are distancing themselves from their previous positions, including Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, who is up for reëlection in November, and used to champion data centers. Last week, he signed an executive order that he claimed “enacted the strictest requirements IN THE NATION” for data-center permits. “We will not be bulldozed by the lawyers for these big tech companies.” But nowhere have the politics of data centers been more strained than in the Wisconsin governor’s race. Earlier this month, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley narrowly won the Democratic nomination after one of the most chaotic and unusual primaries in the state’s history. The front-runner through most of the primary had been Francesca Hong, a democratic-socialist assemblywoman from Madison whose success was partially driven by her vociferous opposition to data centers; her signature policy proposal during the campaign was a one-year moratorium on new data centers, which none of her opponents supported. (In July, Governor Kathy Hochul made New York the first state to enact such a policy.) Hong also called for cutting state funding and tax breaks for companies that lay off workers as a result of adopting A.I. She lost to Crowley by fewer than four thousand votes after attacks from a hostile Democratic establishment; a disastrous appearance on CNN in which she did not walk back a 2020 tweet calling to “cancel Thanksgiving”; and a stream of late money into Crowley’s campaign, including from building-trades unions, who support data centers because of the jobs that they’ll create for their members. Shortly after he beat Hong, Crowley was asked what the biggest difference between them was. He answered, “data centers,” then went on to explain that, while he’s for “guardrails” on them, he is against Hong’s moratorium, because it doesn’t address existing data centers. It was a curious issue for Crowley to single out, especially if he was hoping to attract Hong voters. And, while most politicians who have opposed data centers have been Democrats, Crowley’s Republican opponent, Representative Tom Tiffany, saw a populist opening and pounced. He posted an edited clip of the interview, and the issue soon became the centerpiece of his campaign. (It is the only specific policy currently detailed on his website.) He dubbed Crowley “Data Center David,” and ran ads with a clip from a primary forum in which Crowley said, “There’s an opportunity for us to really become an A.I. and a data hub not only for the entire country but for the entire globe.” In the years since the exemptions went into effect, Wisconsin has become a major hub of data-center construction. More than forty-six billion dollars’ worth of data-center-development projects are currently under construction or being considered in the state, according to an estimate by the nonprofit newsroom Wisconsin Watch. Recently, a Seattle-based company called Cloverleaf Infrastructure has been drawing national attention as “A.I. prospectors” in Wisconsin—securing large plots of land from farmers and other landowners for tech companies. Its biggest success so far is facilitating the development of Oracle and OpenAI’s fifteen-billion-dollar data-center campus in Port Washington, a small town in southeastern Wisconsin. Hyper-scale data centers often demand new natural-gas power plants and transmission lines, and Wisconsin’s Public Service Commission approves or denies permits for such developments, with no requirement for input from local communities. Recently, the commission predicted that the state’s power-generation needs will rise by forty per cent in the next six years, largely because of data centers. Seventy-eight per cent of Wisconsin’s residents now oppose data centers, according to an August poll from Marquette University Law School, up from fifty-five per cent this past October. “Republicans have become more opposed, but Democrats have become even more opposed,” Charles Franklin, the poll’s director, told me. The Marquette poll also showed similar levels of opposition across the state, even in places where there is no proposed development. There are no plans for data centers in the assembly district of Ben Gruber, a Democratic assembly candidate in southwestern Wisconsin, but he has found that the issue still resonates with voters. “Data centers are a physical target of an emotional, visceral populist anger,” Gruber told me. “What everybody is most upset about is the corporate welfare, while our communities suffer,” he said. Since Tiffany’s attacks began, Crowley has moved in Hong’s general direction, emphasizing his requirements—using exclusively renewable energy to power new data centers, building them with union labor—for developers to receive the tax breaks. But he has stopped short of calling for repealing those exemptions, giving Tiffany an opening to try and gain a populist edge on the issue. Last week, Tiffany, who grew up on a dairy farm, embarked on a tour called “Protecting Wisconsin Farmland,” continuing to cultivate his image as a folksy, rural Wisconsinite devoted to beloved institutions like the family farm and the tavern. (One treacly campaign sign reads “You Betcha! Tom Tiffany for Governor.”) His data-center-focussed attack ads emphasize that message.

sources.title: As data centers remain potent political issue, David Crowley offers plan to regulate artificial intelligence in Wisconsin - Wisconsin Watch
passages: In a governor’s race that has focused more on data center construction than artificial intelligence technology, Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley on Tuesday announced a plan for state regulations on AI aimed at protecting vulnerable Wisconsinites.
In an 11-point plan shared with Wisconsin Watch, Crowley calls for guardrails on AI offerings for minors and holding technology companies responsible for scams and fraud on their platforms.
Brittany Carloni joined Wisconsin Watch as the state government and politics reporter in September 2025.

coreStoryFacts.text: MADISON – The two major candidates running to be Wisconsin’s next governor are battling to gain the upper hand on an emerging issue that neither political party owns yet: data centers.
The next governor will undoubtedly reckon with the construction boom in the Badger State of the increasingly controversial factories of artificial intelligence.

As more massive technology centers are stood up across the state, Wisconsin voters of all political stripes are growing more opposed to them, with nearly 80% of voters saying in a recent statewide poll that the costs of building data centers outweigh the benefits.
“There should be full transparency, and we will ban NDAs that keep communities in the dark,” Tiffany told the Journal Sentinel.

Both candidates also said they want the companies that build the data centers to pay for their own energy. “Any costs created by data centers must be paid by the facilities themselves, not passed on to Wisconsin families and businesses through higher utility bills, and they must adhere to the Ratepayer Protection Pledge and bring their own energy,” Tiffany said, referring to an order issued by President Donald Trump on data center regulation.

Tiffany is calling to end tax incentives outright while Crowley said he would make it harder to get them.

The next governor will undoubtedly reckon with the construction boom in the Badger State of the increasingly controversial factories of artificial intelligence. As more massive technology centers are stood up across the state, Wisconsin voters of all political stripes are growing more opposed to them, with nearly 80% of voters saying in a recent statewide poll that the costs of building data centers outweigh the benefits. Democrat David Crowley and Republican Tom Tiffany are each seeking to portray the other as friendlier to big tech, with Tiffany placing seven figures worth of ads across the state dubbing his opponent as “Data Center David Crowley,” and Crowley pointing to Tiffany’s voting record on federal legislation that sought to make it easier to build projects like data centers. Former Democratic candidate Francesca Hong built a formidable following during the primary race, in part, because she called for a moratorium on construction of new data centers in the state ? the only candidate to do so. Crowley and Tiffany are opposed to statewide moratoriums but are calling for stricter regulations governing how such developments may move forward. The starkest contrast between the two is related to the giant carrot state governments can offer data center builders: tax subsidies. Tiffany is calling to end tax incentives outright while Crowley said he would make it harder to get them. Both agree on banning non-disclosure agreements, disagree on subsidies Both Crowley and Tiffany said they would not seek to override the right of local communities to reject developments if they don’t want them. And both said they would seek to ban developers’ use of non-disclosure agreements that keep project details from the public. “These data centers are being built by big tech and we know how these companies try to use our data and hide their motives,” Crowley said in response to a series of questions from the Journal Sentinel about each candidate’s positions on data centers. “If they are building to benefit our communities then they should have nothing to hide. Everything they do should be done so with oversight and public transparency.” “There should be full transparency, and we will ban NDAs that keep communities in the dark,” Tiffany told the Journal Sentinel. Both candidates also said they want the companies that build the data centers to pay for their own energy. “Any costs created by data centers must be paid by the facilities themselves, not passed on to Wisconsin families and businesses through higher utility bills, and they must adhere to the Ratepayer Protection Pledge and bring their own energy,” Tiffany said, referring to an order issued by President Donald Trump on data center regulation. extraction.body: Gorman, who has been on the Rock County Board of Supervisors since 2024, began organizing with citizens across the county who feared that the project would raise utility bills, diminish air quality, and drain the county’s groundwater, joining a growing nationwide backlash against data centers. “I’ve never seen engagement like this on any normal development issue,” Gorman said. “People don’t like that they didn’t have a vote on whether social media could take over our society. And now people see A.I. getting ready to take things over and potentially upset lives, upset society, upset jobs, and they want the ability to have a say in that.” Local residents helped set up informal community meetings to discuss the data center at the public library, and opposition kept building. “I won very conservative parts of the town of Beloit that I had previously lost, purely on the data-center issue,” he told me. “You can knock seven doors and hear seven different reasons why people don’t want this.” A recent Gallup poll found that more than seventy per cent of Americans oppose data centers in their area. And, during the past several weeks, data centers have become increasingly toxic in midterm elections across the country. Opposition has become particularly central to contests in Rust Belt states, such as Republican-trending Ohio, where anti-data-center policies have appeared to boost the campaigns of the Democrats Amy Acton, who is running for governor, and Sherrod Brown, who is running for Senate. Brown’s opponent is the incumbent Jon Husted, who previously, as lieutenant governor, helped usher in an explosion of data centers in the state, many of which were developed after Ohio offered them lucrative tax breaks. Brown’s ability to hammer Husted on this issue is alarming Republican operatives, who see a Husted victory as crucial to holding a majority in the Senate. This month, Axios released a private memo from the National Republican Senatorial Committee warning that data centers have become an “anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.” Other politicians are distancing themselves from their previous positions, including Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, who is up for reëlection in November, and used to champion data centers. Last week, he signed an executive order that he claimed “enacted the strictest requirements IN THE NATION” for data-center permits. “We will not be bulldozed by the lawyers for these big tech companies.” But nowhere have the politics of data centers been more strained than in the Wisconsin governor’s race. Earlier this month, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley narrowly won the Democratic nomination after one of the most chaotic and unusual primaries in the state’s history. The front-runner through most of the primary had been Francesca Hong, a democratic-socialist assemblywoman from Madison whose success was partially driven by her vociferous opposition to data centers; her signature policy proposal during the campaign was a one-year moratorium on new data centers, which none of her opponents supported. (In July, Governor Kathy Hochul made New York the first state to enact such a policy.) Hong also called for cutting state funding and tax breaks for companies that lay off workers as a result of adopting A.I. She lost to Crowley by fewer than four thousand votes after attacks from a hostile Democratic establishment; a disastrous appearance on CNN in which she did not walk back a 2020 tweet calling to “cancel Thanksgiving”; and a stream of late money into Crowley’s campaign, including from building-trades unions, who support data centers because of the jobs that they’ll create for their members. Shortly after he beat Hong, Crowley was asked what the biggest difference between them was. He answered, “data centers,” then went on to explain that, while he’s for “guardrails” on them, he is against Hong’s moratorium, because it doesn’t address existing data centers. It was a curious issue for Crowley to single out, especially if he was hoping to attract Hong voters. And, while most politicians who have opposed data centers have been Democrats, Crowley’s Republican opponent, Representative Tom Tiffany, saw a populist opening and pounced. He posted an edited clip of the interview, and the issue soon became the centerpiece of his campaign. (It is the only specific policy currently detailed on his website.) He dubbed Crowley “Data Center David,” and ran ads with a clip from a primary forum in which Crowley said, “There’s an opportunity for us to really become an A.I. and a data hub not only for the entire country but for the entire globe.” In the years since the exemptions went into effect, Wisconsin has become a major hub of data-center construction. More than forty-six billion dollars’ worth of data-center-development projects are currently under construction or being considered in the state, according to an estimate by the nonprofit newsroom Wisconsin Watch. Recently, a Seattle-based company called Cloverleaf Infrastructure has been drawing national attention as “A.I. prospectors” in Wisconsin—securing large plots of land from farmers and other landowners for tech companies. Its biggest success so far is facilitating the development of Oracle and OpenAI’s fifteen-billion-dollar data-center campus in Port Washington, a small town in southeastern Wisconsin. Hyper-scale data centers often demand new natural-gas power plants and transmission lines, and Wisconsin’s Public Service Commission approves or denies permits for such developments, with no requirement for input from local communities. Recently, the commission predicted that the state’s power-generation needs will rise by forty per cent in the next six years, largely because of data centers. Seventy-eight per cent of Wisconsin’s residents now oppose data centers, according to an August poll from Marquette University Law School, up from fifty-five per cent this past October. “Republicans have become more opposed, but Democrats have become even more opposed,” Charles Franklin, the poll’s director, told me. The Marquette poll also showed similar levels of opposition across the state, even in places where there is no proposed development. There are no plans for data centers in the assembly district of Ben Gruber, a Democratic assembly candidate in southwestern Wisconsin, but he has found that the issue still resonates with voters. “Data centers are a physical target of an emotional, visceral populist anger,” Gruber told me. “What everybody is most upset about is the corporate welfare, while our communities suffer,” he said. Since Tiffany’s attacks began, Crowley has moved in Hong’s general direction, emphasizing his requirements—using exclusively renewable energy to power new data centers, building them with union labor—for developers to receive the tax breaks. But he has stopped short of calling for repealing those exemptions, giving Tiffany an opening to try and gain a populist edge on the issue. Last week, Tiffany, who grew up on a dairy farm, embarked on a tour called “Protecting Wisconsin Farmland,” continuing to cultivate his image as a folksy, rural Wisconsinite devoted to beloved institutions like the family farm and the tavern. (One treacly campaign sign reads “You Betcha! Tom Tiffany for Governor.”) His data-center-focussed attack ads emphasize that message.

passages: In a governor’s race that has focused more on data center construction than artificial intelligence technology, Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley on Tuesday announced a plan for state regulations on AI aimed at protecting vulnerable Wisconsinites.
In an 11-point plan shared with Wisconsin Watch, Crowley calls for guardrails on AI offerings for minors and holding technology companies responsible for scams and fraud on their platforms.
Brittany Carloni joined Wisconsin Watch as the state government and politics reporter in September 2025.
She returned home to Wisconsin after more than eight years away from the Badger State.
Brittany is originally from the Milwaukee area and holds a bachelor’s degree in journalism from Marquette University.

extraction.body: In a governor’s race that has focused more on data center construction than artificial intelligence technology, Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley on Tuesday announced a plan for state regulations on AI aimed at protecting vulnerable Wisconsinites. In an 11-point plan shared with Wisconsin Watch, Crowley calls for guardrails on AI offerings for minors and holding technology companies responsible for scams and fraud on their platforms. Some key components of the plan include: Crowley, the Milwaukee county executive, is running for governor against Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany in what polling from Marquette University Law School shows could be another close governor’s race in Wisconsin. AI policy debates between the two candidates in the months since the August primary have mostly been focused on the planning and construction of AI data centers, rather than the technology itself. In a statement, Tiffany also said Wisconsin needs “commonsense guardrails” to protect children and older adults, including holding companies accountable for platforms that allow creation of sexually explicit images or engage minors in inappropriate chatbot conversations. Tiffany said he also wants to prevent personal data from “falling into the hands of foreign adversaries, including Communist China.” “As governor, I will also support commonsense age-verification requirements for app providers, strengthen parental-consent protections, and give parents greater control over their children’s online activity,” Tiffany said. Crowley’s proposed state-level AI regulations land as President Donald Trump has dismissed calls for guardrails and warnings from technology company leaders asking for government oversight as their platforms become more advanced. Trump in May 2025 signed the Take it Down Act, which criminalized the online publication of real and AI-generated intimate images and requires social media platforms to remove them once notified of their existence. Tiffany, and the rest of Wisconsin’s congressional delegation, voted for the bill in 2025. Other proposed federal legislation has not advanced, including bills requiring public reporting of safety incidents by AI companies and requiring labels on any AI-generated content. Crowley in a statement said he would not “wait around for DC to act” on additional AI regulations if he is elected. “Like so many parents, Ericka and I are raising our three girls in the age of social media and AI, and we’re navigating things no generation before us has ever had to, worrying about whether a stranger is messaging our kids, or a fake picture of our daughter is going around school, or even scammers trying to drain a grandparent’s life savings,” Crowley said. The proposals in Crowley’s regulatory plan would require state legislative action. They echo recent bipartisan efforts signed into law by Gov. Tony Evers, including a series of bills that classified sextortion as a crime and provided additional recourse for victims and their families. Additionally, Attorney General Josh Kaul in August announced Wisconsin could receive up to $313 million in a settlement social media company Meta made with 47 states in a case that alleged addictive components of its platforms threatened teens’ mental health. The next governor will undoubtedly reckon with the construction boom in the Badger State of the increasingly controversial factories of artificial intelligence.

As more massive technology centers are stood up across the state, Wisconsin voters of all political stripes are growing more opposed to them, with nearly 80% of voters saying in a recent statewide poll that the costs of building data centers outweigh the benefits.
“There should be full transparency, and we will ban NDAs that keep communities in the dark,” Tiffany told the Journal Sentinel.

passages: Microsoft has introduced a new hardware security module designed to boost cloud security by enabling cryptographic key protection directly within server environments.
Azure Integrated HSM addresses latency and scalability challenges often associated with traditional network-attached HSMs while adhering to FIPS 140-3 Level 3 security requirements.
The new hardware module provides locally attached cryptographic services for encryption, decryption, signing, and verification.
Keys remain isolated from software, including guest and host systems, ensuring strong physical and logical tamper protection.
This deployment is part of the Secure Future Initiative, which also includes Adams Bridge quantum-resilient accelerator and Caliptra 2.0 silicon root of trust.
The module is designed to integrate seamlessly with both confidential and general-purpose virtual machines and containers, providing dedicated, secure partitions for each workload.
These partitions are hardware-isolated, allowing workloads to access keys only through controlled oracle functions.
This design boosts security and reduces latency with node-integrated connections and cryptographic hardware accelerators.

"As part of our systems approach in optimizing every layer in our infrastructure, security is a key priority, and we are designing our infrastructure hardware with multiple layers of defense with dedicated innovations to ensure robust protection for Microsoft and for our customers," noted Mark Russinovich, Microsoft’s CTO for Azure.

extraction.body: Marvell Technology, Microsoft and Oracle announced a collaborative effort aligned with the Open Compute Project (OCP) aimed at standardizing a NIST FIPS 140-3 Level 3 integrated HSM for cloud and hyperscale data center infrastructure. To direct this effort, the three companies have established a new OCP working group under OCP’s Security Track. The working group’s charter is to define open specifications for an integrated hardware security module for secure key caching and cryptographic key lifecycle management directly at the server level. This approach will reduce latency, improve scalability and strengthen the security posture of cloud compute workloads. Most cloud and enterprise servers today rely on network-attached hardware security modules (HSMs) or software-only key management. This approach requires cryptographic keys to traverse the network or reside in unprotected, non-FIPS 140-3 Level 3 memory, exposing sensitive keys to potential security attacks. The working group will define an open specification for embedding a hardware security boundary, key vault and attestation chain directly into the server. This will ensure that cryptographic operations execute where data is processed, keys never leave a certified hardware boundary and workload integrity can be proven cryptographically to any relying party. Cary Ussery, senior vice president and general manager, Multimarket Business Group, at Marvell An integrated HSM will allow cryptographic key operations to execute where the workload runs, satisfying both regulatory compliance and zero-trust architecture requirements, all without compromising higher performance for security. By defining this as an open specification, we’ll make that capability available to the entire industry. Mark Russinovich, CTO, deputy CISO and technical fellow, Microsoft Azure As AI transforms cybersecurity and quantum technology reshapes cryptography, protecting the keys and credentials at the heart of our digital infrastructure has never been more important. Through the Open Compute Project, industry leaders are coming together around a fully open-source integrated HSM, combining our collective innovation to advance interoperability, accelerate the adoption of post-quantum cryptography, and shape the future of hardware security. Pradeep Vincent, executive vice president, Compute and AI Infrastructure at Oracle An open specification for integrated Hardware Security Module (HSM) capabilities is an important step toward enabling cryptographic operations where data is processed, protecting keys within a hardware security boundary and supporting cryptographic verification of workload integrity. extraction.body: Discover what’s coming to Microsoft Ignite, Nov 17-20, 2026. Register now. At this year’s OCP Global Summit , Microsoft announced Project Tessera, the evolution of the Azure Integrated Hardware Security Module (HSM), into a fully open-source initiative developed in collaboration with Marvell®, Oracle, and Open Compute Project (OCP) . Project Tessera advances our broader commitment to open, industrywide standards for platform security. The motivation behind Project Tessera is straightforward: the entire industry benefits when we collaborate and advance hardware security together. Project Tessera carries forward the workload directly attached to the HSM architecture introduced by Azure Integrated HSM, making the architecture, specifications, protocols, drivers, software, firmware, and reproducible build environments open source for the broader community. Over time, the initiative will advance toward a fully open-source silicon implementation, while making hardware broadly available, enabling organizations across the ecosystem to adopt, integrate, and contribute to the platform. This approach builds on the model Microsoft established with other industry collaborators on Caliptra , a fully open-source silicon root-of-trust that has since been broadly adopted across the hardware ecosystem. Through Project Tessera, industry leaders including Microsoft, Marvell®, Oracle, and the Open Compute Project will apply that same model of transparency and collaboration to advance hardware key protection with the industry. The cybersecurity landscape is rapidly changing, and protecting keys and credentials has never been more important. We are now facing two generational transformations that are fundamentally reshaping how we view the cybersecurity landscape: These emerging threats motivated the development of Azure Integrated HSM , which was designed to meet rigorous security standards for hardware-based key protection, while also accelerating Microsoft’s transition to post-quantum cryptography through scale deployments of quantum resilient integrated HSMs. Azure Integrated HSM introduced a workload-attached HSM that performs cryptographic operations closer to the workload while keys remain continuously protected within the HSM security boundary. This architecture strengthens key protection, improves cryptographic performance, offers crypto-agility, and provides a simpler operational model. Tessera is an evolution of Azure’s first integrated HSM model, incorporating insights gained from deploying Azure Integrated HSM at scale, and advances the technology through collaboration in the Open Compute Project, with the goal of broadly addressing the challenges of key and credential management in the era of AI and quantum computing. In central HSM deployment models, HSM infrastructure is separate from compute resources, requiring cryptographic operations to traverse the network. The resulting latency and operational dependencies can lead enterprises to adopt workarounds that improve performance or availability but unintentionally weaken key protections. Some of these common key-management anti-patterns include: Other anti-patterns include caching keys outside of HSMs for resilience, using software-held keys to reduce network latency to remote HSMs, sharing keys and security domains to simplify governance, and relying on proprietary protocols for interoperability. These practices intend to prioritize operational flexibility but can make key protection, policy enforcement, and auditable provenance less consistent across environments, undermining the security value HSMs are designed to provide. The goal of Project Tessera is to advance the integrated HSM model to address these challenges in the industry, without compromising on security. The project will deliver Tessera Integrated HSM, a fully open-source integrated HSM designed to consistently enforce FIPS 140-3 Level 3 key protection throughout the key’s lifecycle. By combining strong hardware-rooted protection with an open-source implementation and open protocols, Tessera Integrated HSM creates a path toward greater transparency, interoperability, and innovation across the HSM ecosystem . The native support for quantum-resilient cryptography will help ease the industry’s transition to post-quantum cryptography. Today at the Open Compute Project Global Summit, Microsoft and Marvell® demonstrated the Tessera Integrated HSM transfer protocols establishing HSM partition cloning and resiliency rings across a Tessera Integrated HSM and a Marvell® LiquidSecurity® 2 HSM. The demonstration showed how two heterogeneous HSMs can operate in a resilient and unified security domain. Non-extractable keys within the security domain always remain protected within the HSMs and are available only to the authorized HSM partitions participating in the security domain and remain under the sole control of the partition owner. The Tessera Integrated HSM protocols use post-quantum cryptography to protect communication between HSMs. This enables authorized workloads with a Tessera Integrated HSM to use both classical cryptography and post-quantum cryptographic services while their keys remain secured within the HSM boundary and can only be authorized for use by the key owner. The Project Tessera specifications, protocols, software libraries, drivers, firmware, and hardware are available through the Tessera Integrated HSM GitHub . Going forward, this repository will add more open-source silicon, new hardware designs, and enhancements developed with the community. The early collaborators working on Project Tessera within the OCP community are exploring how the Tessera Integrated HSM key protection architecture can extend beyond systems with dedicated integrated HSM hardware. As part of this work, the project is making a minimal, unikernel-based Tessera firmware stack open source, designed to run within hardware-isolated confidential computing environments . This implementation uses the same firmware stack as the hardware integrated HSM, extending a common security architecture across HSMs and confidential computing environments. In this model, cryptographic keys are protected within a confidential computing container, which provides cryptographic services to securely bound workloads, including worker containers and virtual machines. The initial implementation leverages AMD SEV-SNP and integrates with open-source virtualization technologies such as OpenVMM , with the Open Compute community working to extend support to other confidential computing architectures. The complementary deployment models in Project Tessera extend strong key protection across systems with different hardware capabilities and assurance requirements. For platforms without dedicated integrated HSM hardware, confidential computing provides broadly deployable, hardware-isolated key protection with a minimal trusted computing base. Project Tessera provides the highest level of hardware assurance, protecting keys within a dedicated, tamper-resistant security boundary designed to meet demanding certification requirements, including FIPS 140-3 Level 3 and Common Criteria. The deployment models share the same Project Tessera firmware and programming model, giving organizations a consistent foundation for cryptographic security across their infrastructure while providing a natural path to integrated HSM and higher levels of assurance in newer systems. Together, these models make strong key protection accessible across a broad range of systems with different security assurance needs, all built on a common, open architecture. As the Open Compute Project community continues to advance Tessera Integrated HSM, we see an exciting opportunity for broader industry collaboration to strengthen key protection, expand secure key management, and accelerate innovation across the ecosystem. For more information, visit the Microsoft booth at the Open Compute Project Global Summit for live demonstrations, explore Tessera Integrated HSM implementation on GitHub , and read the Microsoft Infrastructure Community blog for additional hardware security announcements: OCP2026 Hardware Security Updates . coreStoryFacts.text: Microsoft has introduced a new hardware security module designed to boost cloud security by enabling cryptographic key protection directly within server environments.
Azure Integrated HSM addresses latency and scalability challenges often associated with traditional network-attached HSMs while adhering to FIPS 140-3 Level 3 security requirements.
The new hardware module provides locally attached cryptographic services for encryption, decryption, signing, and verification.
Keys remain isolated from software, including guest and host systems, ensuring strong physical and logical tamper protection.
This deployment is part of the Secure Future Initiative, which also includes Adams Bridge quantum-resilient accelerator and Caliptra 2.0 silicon root of trust.
The module is designed to integrate seamlessly with both confidential and general-purpose virtual machines and containers, providing dedicated, secure partitions for each workload.
These partitions are hardware-isolated, allowing workloads to access keys only through controlled oracle functions.
This design boosts security and reduces latency with node-integrated connections and cryptographic hardware accelerators.

"As part of our systems approach in optimizing every layer in our infrastructure, security is a key priority, and we are designing our infrastructure hardware with multiple layers of defense with dedicated innovations to ensure robust protection for Microsoft and for our customers," noted Mark Russinovich, Microsoft’s CTO for Azure.

extraction.body: Marvell Technology, Microsoft and Oracle announced a collaborative effort aligned with the Open Compute Project (OCP) aimed at standardizing a NIST FIPS 140-3 Level 3 integrated HSM for cloud and hyperscale data center infrastructure. To direct this effort, the three companies have established a new OCP working group under OCP’s Security Track. The working group’s charter is to define open specifications for an integrated hardware security module for secure key caching and cryptographic key lifecycle management directly at the server level. This approach will reduce latency, improve scalability and strengthen the security posture of cloud compute workloads. Most cloud and enterprise servers today rely on network-attached hardware security modules (HSMs) or software-only key management. This approach requires cryptographic keys to traverse the network or reside in unprotected, non-FIPS 140-3 Level 3 memory, exposing sensitive keys to potential security attacks. The working group will define an open specification for embedding a hardware security boundary, key vault and attestation chain directly into the server. This will ensure that cryptographic operations execute where data is processed, keys never leave a certified hardware boundary and workload integrity can be proven cryptographically to any relying party. Cary Ussery, senior vice president and general manager, Multimarket Business Group, at Marvell An integrated HSM will allow cryptographic key operations to execute where the workload runs, satisfying both regulatory compliance and zero-trust architecture requirements, all without compromising higher performance for security. By defining this as an open specification, we’ll make that capability available to the entire industry. Mark Russinovich, CTO, deputy CISO and technical fellow, Microsoft Azure As AI transforms cybersecurity and quantum technology reshapes cryptography, protecting the keys and credentials at the heart of our digital infrastructure has never been more important. Through the Open Compute Project, industry leaders are coming together around a fully open-source integrated HSM, combining our collective innovation to advance interoperability, accelerate the adoption of post-quantum cryptography, and shape the future of hardware security. extraction.body: Discover what’s coming to Microsoft Ignite, Nov 17-20, 2026. Register now. At this year’s OCP Global Summit , Microsoft announced Project Tessera, the evolution of the Azure Integrated Hardware Security Module (HSM), into a fully open-source initiative developed in collaboration with Marvell®, Oracle, and Open Compute Project (OCP) . Project Tessera advances our broader commitment to open, industrywide standards for platform security. The motivation behind Project Tessera is straightforward: the entire industry benefits when we collaborate and advance hardware security together. Project Tessera carries forward the workload directly attached to the HSM architecture introduced by Azure Integrated HSM, making the architecture, specifications, protocols, drivers, software, firmware, and reproducible build environments open source for the broader community. Over time, the initiative will advance toward a fully open-source silicon implementation, while making hardware broadly available, enabling organizations across the ecosystem to adopt, integrate, and contribute to the platform. This approach builds on the model Microsoft established with other industry collaborators on Caliptra , a fully open-source silicon root-of-trust that has since been broadly adopted across the hardware ecosystem. Through Project Tessera, industry leaders including Microsoft, Marvell®, Oracle, and the Open Compute Project will apply that same model of transparency and collaboration to advance hardware key protection with the industry. The cybersecurity landscape is rapidly changing, and protecting keys and credentials has never been more important. We are now facing two generational transformations that are fundamentally reshaping how we view the cybersecurity landscape: These emerging threats motivated the development of Azure Integrated HSM , which was designed to meet rigorous security standards for hardware-based key protection, while also accelerating Microsoft’s transition to post-quantum cryptography through scale deployments of quantum resilient integrated HSMs. Azure Integrated HSM introduced a workload-attached HSM that performs cryptographic operations closer to the workload while keys remain continuously protected within the HSM security boundary. This architecture strengthens key protection, improves cryptographic performance, offers crypto-agility, and provides a simpler operational model. Tessera is an evolution of Azure’s first integrated HSM model, incorporating insights gained from deploying Azure Integrated HSM at scale, and advances the technology through collaboration in the Open Compute Project, with the goal of broadly addressing the challenges of key and credential management in the era of AI and quantum computing. In central HSM deployment models, HSM infrastructure is separate from compute resources, requiring cryptographic operations to traverse the network. The resulting latency and operational dependencies can lead enterprises to adopt workarounds that improve performance or availability but unintentionally weaken key protections. Some of these common key-management anti-patterns include: Other anti-patterns include caching keys outside of HSMs for resilience, using software-held keys to reduce network latency to remote HSMs, sharing keys and security domains to simplify governance, and relying on proprietary protocols for interoperability. These practices intend to prioritize operational flexibility but can make key protection, policy enforcement, and auditable provenance less consistent across environments, undermining the security value HSMs are designed to provide. The goal of Project Tessera is to advance the integrated HSM model to address these challenges in the industry, without compromising on security. The project will deliver Tessera Integrated HSM, a fully open-source integrated HSM designed to consistently enforce FIPS 140-3 Level 3 key protection throughout the key’s lifecycle. By combining strong hardware-rooted protection with an open-source implementation and open protocols, Tessera Integrated HSM creates a path toward greater transparency, interoperability, and innovation across the HSM ecosystem . The native support for quantum-resilient cryptography will help ease the industry’s transition to post-quantum cryptography. Today at the Open Compute Project Global Summit, Microsoft and Marvell® demonstrated the Tessera Integrated HSM transfer protocols establishing HSM partition cloning and resiliency rings across a Tessera Integrated HSM and a Marvell® LiquidSecurity® 2 HSM. The demonstration showed how two heterogeneous HSMs can operate in a resilient and unified security domain. Non-extractable keys within the security domain always remain protected within the HSMs and are available only to the authorized HSM partitions participating in the security domain and remain under the sole control of the partition owner. The Tessera Integrated HSM protocols use post-quantum cryptography to protect communication between HSMs. This enables authorized workloads with a Tessera Integrated HSM to use both classical cryptography and post-quantum cryptographic services while their keys remain secured within the HSM boundary and can only be authorized for use by the key owner. The Project Tessera specifications, protocols, software libraries, drivers, firmware, and hardware are available through the Tessera Integrated HSM GitHub . Going forward, this repository will add more open-source silicon, new hardware designs, and enhancements developed with the community. The early collaborators working on Project Tessera within the OCP community are exploring how the Tessera Integrated HSM key protection architecture can extend beyond systems with dedicated integrated HSM hardware. As part of this work, the project is making a minimal, unikernel-based Tessera firmware stack open source, designed to run within hardware-isolated confidential computing environments . This implementation uses the same firmware stack as the hardware integrated HSM, extending a common security architecture across HSMs and confidential computing environments. In this model, cryptographic keys are protected within a confidential computing container, which provides cryptographic services to securely bound workloads, including worker containers and virtual machines. The initial implementation leverages AMD SEV-SNP and integrates with open-source virtualization technologies such as OpenVMM , with the Open Compute community working to extend support to other confidential computing architectures. The complementary deployment models in Project Tessera extend strong key protection across systems with different hardware capabilities and assurance requirements. For platforms without dedicated integrated HSM hardware, confidential computing provides broadly deployable, hardware-isolated key protection with a minimal trusted computing base. Project Tessera provides the highest level of hardware assurance, protecting keys within a dedicated, tamper-resistant security boundary designed to meet demanding certification requirements, including FIPS 140-3 Level 3 and Common Criteria. The deployment models share the same Project Tessera firmware and programming model, giving organizations a consistent foundation for cryptographic security across their infrastructure while providing a natural path to integrated HSM and higher levels of assurance in newer systems. Together, these models make strong key protection accessible across a broad range of systems with different security assurance needs, all built on a common, open architecture. As the Open Compute Project community continues to advance Tessera Integrated HSM, we see an exciting opportunity for broader industry collaboration to strengthen key protection, expand secure key management, and accelerate innovation across the ecosystem. For more information, visit the Microsoft booth at the Open Compute Project Global Summit for live demonstrations, explore Tessera Integrated HSM implementation on GitHub , and read the Microsoft Infrastructure Community blog for additional hardware security announcements: OCP2026 Hardware Security Updates . As part of this work, the project is making a minimal, unikernel-based Tessera firmware stack open source, designed to run within hardware-isolated confidential computing environments .

This implementation uses the same firmware stack as the hardware integrated HSM, extending a common security architecture across HSMs and confidential computing environments. In this model, cryptographic keys are protected within a confidential computing container, which provides cryptographic services to securely bound workloads, including worker containers and virtual machines. The initial implementation leverages AMD SEV-SNP and integrates with open-source virtualization technologies such as OpenVMM , with the Open Compute community working to extend support to other confidential computing architectures.

The complementary deployment models in Project Tessera extend strong key protection across systems with different hardware capabilities and assurance requirements. For platforms without dedicated integrated HSM hardware, confidential computing provides broadly deployable, hardware-isolated key protection with a minimal trusted computing base.

Project Tessera provides the highest level of hardware assurance, protecting keys within a dedicated, tamper-resistant security boundary designed to meet demanding certification requirements, including FIPS 140-3 Level 3 and Common Criteria.

The deployment models share the same Project Tessera firmware and programming model, giving organizations a consistent foundation for cryptographic security across their infrastructure while providing a natural path to integrated HSM and higher levels of assurance in newer systems.

Together, these models make strong key protection accessible across a broad range of systems with different security assurance needs, all built on a common, open architecture. As the Open Compute Project community continues to advance Tessera Integrated HSM, we see an exciting opportunity for broader industry collaboration to strengthen key protection, expand secure key management, and accelerate innovation across the ecosystem.

extraction.body: A London court has ruled that the UK government’s likelihood of retaining most of the seized bitcoins has increased. The related bitcoins are valued at approximately £3.8 billion ($5 billion), following a report by the Financial Times that the court determined thousands of Chinese fraud victims cannot claim these coins under UK law. This case involves 61,000 bitcoins seized by the London Metropolitan Police during their investigation of Zhimin Qian, who has admitted to defrauding thousands of people in China. Qian operated a large-scale Ponzi scheme through her company, Tianjin Lantian Gerui Electronic Technology, defrauding over 128,000 investors between 2014 and 2017. She then converted billions of dollars in stolen funds into Bitcoin and fled to the UK in 2017. The victims had argued that British law should apply, as this might allow them to assert property rights over the billions of pounds in crypto assets. However, on Monday, Judge Mark Turner of the London High Court sided with UK authorities, ruling that Chinese law, not British law, should govern the victims’ property claims, since the underlying fraud occurred entirely in China. The judge stated: "The relevant harm occurred in China. The applicants surrendered their funds in China. The alleged fraudulent representations were made in China. The contractual relationships induced thereby were established in China. The direct economic consequences of the misconduct were also borne in China." However, this ruling does not ultimately determine who will own these bitcoins. But it narrows the path for victims to recover these bitcoins and increases the likelihood that the UK Treasury will ultimately retain the seized bitcoins. According to the Financial Times, the victims' lawyers are appealing. The UK Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) stated that upcoming hearings will determine whether any victims can prove ownership of these bitcoins. Across the Atlantic, seized bitcoins have been institutionalized as part of the national balance sheet. In March 2025, the United States established a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve, which includes BTC and other tokens seized during law enforcement operations. No single token was purchased with taxpayer funds. According to Arkham Intelligence, wallet addresses associated with the U.S. government hold cryptocurrency valued at $25.8 billion.

extraction.body: Your vibe-coded applications can now be easily run on Android smartphones without having to first go public on the Google Play Store, the tech giant announced on Tuesday. A new feature will allow users to launch their own personal apps on their device via Google Play using their standard Google account, but they will remain completely private. These personal apps won’t show up in Google Play’s search or listing pages, and won’t be shared with anyone except for the app’s creator. The idea comes as more people are experimenting with building their own applications via AI for specific, personal needs. However, being able to use that app on their own Android device has meant publishing to Google Play, making it accessible to the Play Store’s some 3 billion users. That led many to limit their vibe-coding efforts to web apps that could run on any device instead of something built natively for Android. Now, Google says Android device owners can vibe-code an app using Google AI Studio, then launch it for their own use. These apps are still required to comply with Google Play’s existing policies but allow users to experiment more directly with building apps for Android. Initially, the feature will be available to users in the U.S., age 18 and up. “That’s why the future of apps on Google Play is personal, secure, and built by everyone — and it’s why Play is leading the charge and moving from ‘there’s an app for that’ to ‘there’s an app for me,’” said Sam Bright, Google’s VP and GM for the Google Play and Developer Ecosystem, in a press briefing ahead of Tuesday’s launch. “We started Google Play with a simple goal: to connect you with the apps you love. But after today, we hope it’s clear: Play has evolved to become so much more than that.” In the months ahead, the company said that users will be able to share their vibe-coded creations with a network of trusted friends. That means the apps you built for family or friends, or maybe your child’s T-ball league, could be used with a small group of people, without having to go public on the Play Store. And if the app ever really becomes popular, there will be a way to shift the personal app to one that’s published on the Google Play Store for everyone to try, after completing the trust and safety reviews. Google will also allow users to curate their own lists of games, post questions about games to a new Community Posts section, and join new 48-hour gaming challenges called Sprints, among other gaming-related feature updates. Plus, the Play Store’s built-in AI assistant, Ask Play, is being updated to offer comparisons, allowing users to see the key differences between similar applications. Google Play apps and games will also be more deeply integrated into Gemini’s conversations. The changes are rolling out alongside Google Play’s new support for an age-range feature that allows parents to share their child’s age range, but not their exact birthdate, with developers to get an age-appropriate experience. extraction.body: Your vibe-coded applications can now be easily run on Android smartphones without having to first go public on the Google Play Store, the tech giant announced on Tuesday. A new feature will allow users to launch their own personal apps on their device via Google Play using their standard Google account, but they will remain completely private. These personal apps won’t show up in Google Play’s search or listing pages, and won’t be shared with anyone except for the app’s creator. The idea comes as more people are experimenting with building their own applications via AI for specific, personal needs. However, being able to use that app on their own Android device has meant publishing to Google Play, making it accessible to the Play Store’s some 3 billion users. That led many to limit their vibe-coding efforts to web apps that could run on any device instead of something built natively for Android. Now, Google says Android device owners can vibe-code an app using Google AI Studio, then launch it for their own use. These apps are still required to comply with Google Play’s existing policies but allow users to experiment more directly with building apps for Android. Initially, the feature will be available to users in the U.S., age 18 and up. “That’s why the future of apps on Google Play is personal, secure, and built by everyone — and it’s why Play is leading the charge and moving from ‘there’s an app for that’ to ‘there’s an app for me,’” said Sam Bright, Google’s VP and GM for the Google Play and Developer Ecosystem, in a press briefing ahead of Tuesday’s launch. “We started Google Play with a simple goal: to connect you with the apps you love. But after today, we hope it’s clear: Play has evolved to become so much more than that.” In the months ahead, the company said that users will be able to share their vibe-coded creations with a network of trusted friends. That means the apps you built for family or friends, or maybe your child’s T-ball league, could be used with a small group of people, without having to go public on the Play Store. And if the app ever really becomes popular, there will be a way to shift the personal app to one that’s published on the Google Play Store for everyone to try, after completing the trust and safety reviews. Google will also allow users to curate their own lists of games, post questions about games to a new Community Posts section, and join new 48-hour gaming challenges called Sprints, among other gaming-related feature updates. Plus, the Play Store’s built-in AI assistant, Ask Play, is being updated to offer comparisons, allowing users to see the key differences between similar applications. Google Play apps and games will also be more deeply integrated into Gemini’s conversations. The changes are rolling out alongside Google Play’s new support for an age-range feature that allows parents to share their child’s age range, but not their exact birthdate, with developers to get an age-appropriate experience. sources.title: Flox Intelligence is building AI to keep wildlife away from trains, airports, and roads
passages: Reading about all that damage, to both infrastructure and animals, inspired Sara Nozkova (pictured above on the left) to develop a wildlife-deterrent system that works differently from the sirens, lights, fences, falcons, and culling traditionally used to keep animals away from roads, train tracks, airports, and other infrastructure.

That work turned into Flox Intelligence , which spun out of KTH in 2020 and is one of the finalists at this year’s Startup Battlefield 200 pitch competition at TechCrunch Disrupt , taking place this year at Moscone West in San Francisco October 13-15.
Like autonomous vehicles, they use perception systems to sense their surroundings, but theirs are trained on wildlife behavior.

extraction.body: When I was eight, I remember our train to Mumbai ground to a halt with a great noise. When we started moving again, a good eight hours later, someone pointed out a mangled tail, of all things, hanging from a branch close to the tracks. The train, you see, had apparently hit a wild bison at full speed, and the impact damaged the engine so badly that it had to be towed away for repairs. For a long time, I thought such things only happened in places like rural India, but I learned a few years ago that wildlife and infrastructure do not mix anywhere on the planet. The FAA estimates that wildlife strikes have cost U.S. civil aviation about $272 million a year on average between 1990 and 2025. In France, the rail operator SNCF says wandering animals affect more than 8,000 trains across the country each year and are among its five leading causes of delays. In Brittany, 120 trains hit animals in 2023 alone, disrupting 660 services and causing more than 15,000 minutes of delays. Reading about all that damage, to both infrastructure and animals, inspired Sara Nozkova (pictured above on the left) to develop a wildlife-deterrent system that works differently from the sirens, lights, fences, falcons, and culling traditionally used to keep animals away from roads, train tracks, airports, and other infrastructure. “I was convinced the answer was not a louder deterrent,” she told TechCrunch. After spending 13 years working in transportation and autonomous vehicles, Nozkova had learned how quickly the systems we build to navigate roads and other controlled environments fail once nature enters the equation. “We have taught machines to be brilliant, but only inside the environments we engineered for them,” she said. “Cities, factory lines, warehouses. Fixed geometry, known objects. Stepping outside into nature, I saw firsthand how the same machines quickly go blind. Because nature is complex and always alive.” So instead she joined the AI lab at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm and started working on a system that could change its deterrent responses based on what an animal nearby is doing, and even what kind of animal it is. That work turned into Flox Intelligence , which spun out of KTH in 2020 and is one of the finalists at this year’s Startup Battlefield 200 pitch competition at TechCrunch Disrupt , taking place this year at Moscone West in San Francisco October 13-15. Flox makes edge devices that process data on-site rather than in the cloud. Like autonomous vehicles, they use perception systems to sense their surroundings, but theirs are trained on wildlife behavior. A motion sensor wakes the device when it detects movement, triggering a camera that uses on-device models to identify nearby animals. The device then emits a species-appropriate sound to scare them away. Nozkova says the system learns from experience, too, and varies its responses so animals don’t get habituated to repeated signals. The company currently sells battery-operated devices that can be mounted on poles, trees, and other structures. It also offers a software platform that shows clients where the devices are deployed and what’s happening on the ground. The platform can also generate reports for regulatory compliance and for uses like biodiversity monitoring. The longer-term goal is to make the software portable enough to run on machines that work outside, including trains, cars, and drones. Nozkova says about 150 Flox devices are live in North America, Europe, and Australia at airfields and airport perimeters, road and rail corridors (especially fence ends and crossings along wildlife corridors), national parks, agricultural land, urban areas, mining sites, and critical infrastructure such as electrical substations. The company sells edge units up front, then charges an annual software and AI subscription after the first year. Flox also has OEM partnerships with companies that pay an annual fee to deploy its software on vehicles, like trains. Train manufacturer Alstom is one such partner. The company expects to end 2026 with revenue of about $1.5 million, Nozkova said. As unique as Flox’s product and approach are, the startup is not without competition. Robin Radar’s Scarecrow also uses species-specific distress calls to disperse birds and it records the activity, while iCHASE sells a system that detects birds with computer vision and targets them with a moving laser, adjusting its response as needed. Nozkova says her moat is the breadth of the system and the data Flox has collected in the field, which she calls “ground truth on what actually makes a moose or a grizzly bear move safely.” “Physical AI is walking out of the factory and into the messy, alive outdoors,” Nozkova says. “Every machine that operates outside — trains, trucks, drones, tractors, robots — will need to understand nature, and nature intelligence is the next layer of the perception stack. Almost nobody is building it.” The company has raised about $5 million across pre-seed and seed rounds so far, with the seed round led by Unconventional Ventures and Tilia Impact Ventures. Co-investors across the rounds include GENIUS NY, Norrsken, Satgana, and angel investors, Nozkova said. The company is now opening a $10 million Series A, which would mostly go toward growing from about 150 devices to several thousand deployed units and extending the underlying system beyond its current wildlife use cases. sources.title: Sweden's Flox Intelligence raises €2.5 million to become a “digital shepherd” guiding wildlife away from danger - EU-Startups
passages: Flox Intelligence , a wildlife intelligence company building AI systems enabling infrastructure to prevent human-wildlife conflict, today announced a €2.5 million ($3 million) Seed+ round to accelerate deployments across North America.
It is building edge-based physical AI that can operate 24/7 in harsh environments, where decisions have to be made in seconds.
The company combines embedded systems, real-time sensing, and applied wildlife science to speak with animals in their own language.
“For decades, we’ve relied on reactive tools — from scare tactics to fences — that don’t scale, don’t learn, and don’t protect the corridors wildlife depends on.
For so many years, we have been fighting wildlife, but what if we could communicate with them instead?

“Flox Intelligence is building a future where critical infrastructure can proactively prevent conflict, where animal movement is respected and safer, and where people and wildlife can finally coexist.

The technology prevents collisions, damage, and disruption across critical infrastructure, including railways, airports, roads, agriculture, and industrial sites, and provides reporting through the Flox Wildlife Platform.
This keeps growing every year as humans take more space, wild animals are pushed closer to urban spaces, and transportation systems get faster, quieter, and harder to avoid.
Flox Intelligence was founded in 2020 by Nozkova and Tomas Becklin.
It was born out of an AI research lab at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm.
The company recently relocated its commercial headquarters to the US.
It is also helping DOT road networks where deer and bison collisions drive injuries, fatalities, and financial losses.
Flox Intelligence claims to be built on a different premise.
It has expanded its operations across the U.S. and Canada, grown its New York headquarters, and accelerated commercial deployments over the past few months.
Ford International Airport, WWF, KWS Group, Boliden, and Alstom.

The startup’s first commercial product, Edge, is an intelligent wildlife deterrent system built for harsh, real-world environments, engineered for multiple species, extreme weather, remote sites, limited connectivity, and long uptime.

Every deployment makes the next one smarter, and collectively, these deployments are building one of the world’s largest non-lethal wildlife datasets and windows into how wildlife moves, adapts, and survives alongside human infrastructure.

The round was led by Tilia Impact Ventures, with participation from Satgana, GENIUS NY (operated by CenterState CEO), J.O.S.S. and existing investors Unconventional Ventures and Almi Invest. Sara Nozkova , CEO and co-founder of Flox Intelligence, said, “The future of infrastructure safety will include wildlife intelligence by default. “For decades, we’ve relied on reactive tools — from scare tactics to fences — that don’t scale, don’t learn, and don’t protect the corridors wildlife depends on. For so many years, we have been fighting wildlife, but what if we could communicate with them instead? “Flox Intelligence is building a future where critical infrastructure can proactively prevent conflict, where animal movement is respected and safer, and where people and wildlife can finally coexist. Our goal is to make wildlife intelligence a standard layer of modern operations — and to lead that category globally.” Flox Intelligence was founded in 2020 by Nozkova and Tomas Becklin. It was born out of an AI research lab at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm. The company recently relocated its commercial headquarters to the US. Flox Intelligence is an AI-powered wildlife intelligence company that aims to create a world where humans and wildlife coexist. According to the company, it builds autonomous systems deployed on the edge that guide wildlife in real time using AI, bioacoustics, and applied wildlife science. The technology prevents collisions, damage, and disruption across critical infrastructure, including railways, airports, roads, agriculture, and industrial sites, and provides reporting through the Flox Wildlife Platform. The company claims to replace reactive, fragmented deterrents like scarecrows, pyrotechnics, gunshots, and fences with a modern, autonomous layer of prevention and learning at the edge. Every deployment makes the next one smarter, and collectively, these deployments are building one of the world’s largest non-lethal wildlife datasets and windows into how wildlife moves, adapts, and survives alongside human infrastructure. Flox Intelligence mentions that human-wildlife conflict is already a global multi-billion-euro problem. This keeps growing every year as humans take more space, wild animals are pushed closer to urban spaces, and transportation systems get faster, quieter, and harder to avoid. According to the company, existing tools do not scale and lack adaptive learning capabilities. Flox Intelligence claims to be built on a different premise. It is building edge-based physical AI that can operate 24/7 in harsh environments, where decisions have to be made in seconds. The company combines embedded systems, real-time sensing, and applied wildlife science to speak with animals in their own language. “In other words, it turns wildlife communication into actionable intelligence — enabling critical infrastructure to “speak” with wildlife and gently guide them away from high-risk zones before incidents happen,” mentioned Flox Intelligence. The startup’s first commercial product, Edge, is an intelligent wildlife deterrent system built for harsh, real-world environments, engineered for multiple species, extreme weather, remote sites, limited connectivity, and long uptime. It is always on, multi-species, multi-modal, and deployed at the edge. Flox Intelligence has already started shipping Edge pods to the front lines of human-wildlife conflict, including airports dealing with coyotes, deer, and bird strike risks, to rail corridors affected by large wildlife such as moose and bears. It is also helping DOT road networks where deer and bison collisions drive injuries, fatalities, and financial losses. Some other use cases of Edge include ranches and farms balancing predator-healthy ecosystems with livestock protection, and cities and public spaces that witness wildlife movement. The company reports that Edge has logged over 60,000 wildlife events across 27 species, and early deployments show measurable reductions in wildlife presence in high-risk zones. This funding follows Flox Intelligence’s Seed round in July last year. It has expanded its operations across the U.S. and Canada, grown its New York headquarters, and accelerated commercial deployments over the past few months. The fresh capital will be used by the company to accelerate deployments across North America. It will also support growing international demand for Flox Intelligence’s AI-powered wildlife deterrence platform across airports, rail corridors, road networks, and industrial sites. Flox Intelligence reports that it already works with major airports, departments of transportation, infrastructure owners, and mission-driven partners across North America and Europe. Its partners include the U.S. Department of Agriculture, GRR Gerald R. Ford International Airport, WWF, KWS Group, Boliden, and Alstom.
