extraction.body: When I was eight, I remember our train to Mumbai ground to a halt with a great noise. When we started moving again, a good eight hours later, someone pointed out a mangled tail, of all things, hanging from a branch close to the tracks. The train, you see, had apparently hit a wild bison at full speed, and the impact damaged the engine so badly that it had to be towed away for repairs. For a long time, I thought such things only happened in places like rural India, but I learned a few years ago that wildlife and infrastructure do not mix anywhere on the planet. The FAA estimates that wildlife strikes have cost U.S. civil aviation about $272 million a year on average between 1990 and 2025. In France, the rail operator SNCF says wandering animals affect more than 8,000 trains across the country each year and are among its five leading causes of delays. In Brittany, 120 trains hit animals in 2023 alone, disrupting 660 services and causing more than 15,000 minutes of delays. Reading about all that damage, to both infrastructure and animals, inspired Sara Nozkova (pictured above on the left) to develop a wildlife-deterrent system that works differently from the sirens, lights, fences, falcons, and culling traditionally used to keep animals away from roads, train tracks, airports, and other infrastructure. “I was convinced the answer was not a louder deterrent,” she told TechCrunch. After spending 13 years working in transportation and autonomous vehicles, Nozkova had learned how quickly the systems we build to navigate roads and other controlled environments fail once nature enters the equation. “We have taught machines to be brilliant, but only inside the environments we engineered for them,” she said. “Cities, factory lines, warehouses. Fixed geometry, known objects. Stepping outside into nature, I saw firsthand how the same machines quickly go blind. Because nature is complex and always alive.” So instead she joined the AI lab at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm and started working on a system that could change its deterrent responses based on what an animal nearby is doing, and even what kind of animal it is. That work turned into Flox Intelligence , which spun out of KTH in 2020 and is one of the finalists at this year’s Startup Battlefield 200 pitch competition at TechCrunch Disrupt , taking place this year at Moscone West in San Francisco October 13-15. Flox makes edge devices that process data on-site rather than in the cloud. Like autonomous vehicles, they use perception systems to sense their surroundings, but theirs are trained on wildlife behavior. A motion sensor wakes the device when it detects movement, triggering a camera that uses on-device models to identify nearby animals. The device then emits a species-appropriate sound to scare them away. Nozkova says the system learns from experience, too, and varies its responses so animals don’t get habituated to repeated signals. The company currently sells battery-operated devices that can be mounted on poles, trees, and other structures. It also offers a software platform that shows clients where the devices are deployed and what’s happening on the ground. The platform can also generate reports for regulatory compliance and for uses like biodiversity monitoring. The longer-term goal is to make the software portable enough to run on machines that work outside, including trains, cars, and drones. Nozkova says about 150 Flox devices are live in North America, Europe, and Australia at airfields and airport perimeters, road and rail corridors (especially fence ends and crossings along wildlife corridors), national parks, agricultural land, urban areas, mining sites, and critical infrastructure such as electrical substations. The company sells edge units up front, then charges an annual software and AI subscription after the first year. Flox also has OEM partnerships with companies that pay an annual fee to deploy its software on vehicles, like trains. Train manufacturer Alstom is one such partner. The company expects to end 2026 with revenue of about $1.5 million, Nozkova said. As unique as Flox’s product and approach are, the startup is not without competition. Robin Radar’s Scarecrow also uses species-specific distress calls to disperse birds and it records the activity, while iCHASE sells a system that detects birds with computer vision and targets them with a moving laser, adjusting its response as needed. Nozkova says her moat is the breadth of the system and the data Flox has collected in the field, which she calls “ground truth on what actually makes a moose or a grizzly bear move safely.” “Physical AI is walking out of the factory and into the messy, alive outdoors,” Nozkova says. “Every machine that operates outside — trains, trucks, drones, tractors, robots — will need to understand nature, and nature intelligence is the next layer of the perception stack. Almost nobody is building it.” The company has raised about $5 million across pre-seed and seed rounds so far, with the seed round led by Unconventional Ventures and Tilia Impact Ventures. Co-investors across the rounds include GENIUS NY, Norrsken, Satgana, and angel investors, Nozkova said. The company is now opening a $10 million Series A, which would mostly go toward growing from about 150 devices to several thousand deployed units and extending the underlying system beyond its current wildlife use cases. Ram is a financial and tech reporter and editor. He covered North American and European M&A, equity, regulatory news and debt markets at Reuters and Acuris Global, and has also written about travel, tourism, entertainment and books. story.title: Flox Intelligence is building AI to keep wildlife away from trains, airports, and roads

facts.text: Reading about all that damage, to both infrastructure and animals, inspired Sara Nozkova (pictured above on the left) to develop a wildlife-deterrent system that works differently from the sirens, lights, fences, falcons, and culling traditionally used to keep animals away from roads, train tracks, airports, and other infrastructure.

That work turned into Flox Intelligence , which spun out of KTH in 2020 and is one of the finalists at this year’s Startup Battlefield 200 pitch competition at TechCrunch Disrupt , taking place this year at Moscone West in San Francisco October 13-15.
Like autonomous vehicles, they use perception systems to sense their surroundings, but theirs are trained on wildlife behavior.

Nozkova says about 150 Flox devices are live in North America, Europe, and Australia at airfields and airport perimeters, road and rail corridors (especially fence ends and crossings along wildlife corridors), national parks, agricultural land, urban areas, mining sites, and critical infrastructure such as electrical substations.
The train, you see, had apparently hit a wild bison at full speed, and the impact damaged the engine so badly that it had to be towed away for repairs.

After spending 13 years working in transportation and autonomous vehicles, Nozkova had learned how quickly the systems we build to navigate roads and other controlled environments fail once nature enters the equation.
Flox also has OEM partnerships with companies that pay an annual fee to deploy its software on vehicles, like trains.

But the data from the very week he made that call tells a very different story. Tom Lee, Chairman of BitMine Immersion Technologies ( NYSEAMERICAN:BMNR | BMNR Price Prediction ), said on October 12, 2026, that he believes tokenization and AI agents will end Ethereum’s ( CRYPTO:ETH ) extended decline against Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ). However, between October 6 and October 13, the ETH/BTC ratio fell another 4.7%, with Ethereum down 8.0% and Bitcoin down 3.5%. Lee also mentioned that this shift could ignite the largest bull market in cryptocurrency history, driven by what he sees as a $2 trillion wealth transfer. This is a bold call from the head of a company that holds more Ethereum than any other. Over the past week, the ETH/BTC ratio, which divides Ethereum’s price by Bitcoin’s price, fell significantly. This ratio indicates how much Bitcoin one Ethereum can buy. As of October 13, with Ethereum priced at around $2,498 and Bitcoin at approximately $83,280, the ratio stands at 0.0300. This direct comparison shows how the two cryptocurrencies are performing against each other, independent of the overall market. Over the past seven days, Bitcoin outperformed Ethereum. A prolonged decline in this ratio negatively impacts a specific group of investors who hold Ethereum in the hope that it will eventually surpass Bitcoin. Many believe that Ethereum’s ability to run applications gives it the edge over Bitcoin, which primarily functions as a store of value. When the ratio declines over the years, these investors would have been better off owning Bitcoin, even during periods when Ethereum’s dollar price increased . Lee’s assertion focuses on future trends rather than specific price points, but the past week hasn’t favored his view. Tokenization refers to transforming assets, like stocks, into digital tokens that can be traded on a blockchain. Agentic AI involves software that can make decisions and handle transactions without human intervention. Both concepts require a blockchain to operate, and Lee believes Ethereum is best positioned to benefit because of its existing ecosystem of developers, applications, and trading activity. If demand for these assets rises, it could drive more Ethereum purchases than Bitcoin, potentially lifting the ETH/BTC ratio. However, the tokenized-stocks market is relatively small, valued at about $3.9 billion compared with Ethereum’s market value of roughly $305 billion. Spot Ethereum ETFs , which directly hold Ethereum and trade like stocks, have faced a concerning trend, recording nine consecutive days of outflows . This means investors have withdrawn more than they have invested each day, with these funds holding $15.86 billion in net assets, according to SoSoValue. BitMine, the largest single buyer of Ethereum, is also slowing its pace. In its latest weekly purchase, the company acquired 12,532 ETH, valued at around $31 million—less than it bought in previous weeks. Additionally, BitMine has a maximum capacity of 77,442 ETH left to buy, around $193 million at current prices, before it reaches 5% of Ethereum’s total supply, at which point purchasing will halt, according to its CEO. Chart analysts also express concern, pointing to a potential head-and-shoulders pattern in Ethereum’s price chart, characterized by three peaks, with the middle peak being the highest. This pattern often signals fading buying interest, though such patterns do not always play out as expected. At this point, it doesn’t seem so yet. The ETH/BTC ratio fell in the past week, investor money has left Ethereum ETFs for nine straight days, and the most consistent buyer is nearing its buying limit. While Lee may be outlining a future shift that could unfold over several quarters, the current data does not support this assertion. A critical test will occur when BitMine exhausts the remaining 77,442 ETH of room under its 5% cap. If the ETH/BTC ratio stays above 0.0300 after that point, it could indicate new buyers are entering the market, bolstering Lee’s case. Positive trends like steady ETF inflows, sustained interest in altcoins , and tokenized stocks significantly surpassing the current $3.9 billion market could lend substantial support to Lee’s case. Conversely, if the ratio dips below 0.0300 after BitMine steps back, it suggests that Ethereum’s long-term decline may still dominate the market narrative. facts.text: Tom Lee predicts tokenization and AI agents will reverse Ethereum's slide against Bitcoin, but the ETH/BTC ratio fell 4.7% that same week.
This ratio indicates how much Bitcoin one Ethereum can buy.
As of October 13, with Ethereum priced at around $2,498 and Bitcoin at approximately $83,280, the ratio stands at 0.0300.
This direct comparison shows how the two cryptocurrencies are performing against each other, independent of the overall market.
Over the past seven days, Bitcoin outperformed Ethereum.
A prolonged decline in this ratio negatively impacts a specific group of investors who hold Ethereum in the hope that it will eventually surpass Bitcoin.
Many believe that Ethereum's ability to run applications gives it the edge over Bitcoin, which primarily functions as a store of value.
When the ratio declines over the years, these investors would have been better off owning Bitcoin, even during periods when Ethereum's dollar price increased.
However, the tokenized-stocks market is relatively small, valued at about $3.9 billion compared with Ethereum's market value of roughly $305 billion.

This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.

Tom Lee, Chairman of BitMine Immersion Technologies ( NYSEAMERICAN:BMNR | BMNR Price Prediction ), said on October 12, 2026, that he believes tokenization and AI agents will end Ethereum’s ( CRYPTO:ETH ) extended decline against Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ). However, between October 6 and October 13, the ETH/BTC ratio fell another 4.7%, with Ethereum down 8.0% and Bitcoin down 3.5%.

Lee also mentioned that this shift could ignite the largest bull market in cryptocurrency history, driven by what he sees as a $2 trillion wealth transfer. This is a bold call from the head of a company that holds more Ethereum than any other.

Over the past week, the ETH/BTC ratio, which divides Ethereum’s price by Bitcoin’s price, fell significantly. This ratio indicates how much Bitcoin one Ethereum can buy. As of October 13, with Ethereum priced at around $2,498 and Bitcoin at approximately $83,280, the ratio stands at 0.0300. This direct comparison shows how the two cryptocurrencies are performing against each other, independent of the overall market. Over the past seven days, Bitcoin outperformed Ethereum.

A prolonged decline in this ratio negatively impacts a specific group of investors who hold Ethereum in the hope that it will eventually surpass Bitcoin. Many believe that Ethereum’s ability to run applications gives it the edge over Bitcoin, which primarily functions as a store of value. When the ratio declines over the years, these investors would have been better off owning Bitcoin, even during periods when Ethereum’s dollar price increased .
Lee’s assertion focuses on future trends rather than specific price points, but the past week hasn’t favored his view.

Tokenization refers to transforming assets, like stocks, into digital tokens that can be traded on a blockchain. Agentic AI involves software that can make decisions and handle transactions without human intervention. Both concepts require a blockchain to operate, and Lee believes Ethereum is best positioned to benefit because of its existing ecosystem of developers, applications, and trading activity.

If demand for these assets rises, it could drive more Ethereum purchases than Bitcoin, potentially lifting the ETH/BTC ratio. However, the tokenized-stocks market is relatively small, valued at about $3.9 billion compared with Ethereum’s market value of roughly $305 billion.

Spot Ethereum ETFs , which directly hold Ethereum and trade like stocks, have faced a concerning trend, recording nine consecutive days of outflows . This means investors have withdrawn more than they have invested each day, with these funds holding $15.86 billion in net assets, according to SoSoValue.

BitMine, the largest single buyer of Ethereum, is also slowing its pace. In its latest weekly purchase, the company acquired 12,532 ETH, valued at around $31 million—less than it bought in previous weeks. Additionally, BitMine has a maximum capacity of 77,442 ETH left to buy, around $193 million at current prices, before it reaches 5% of Ethereum’s total supply, at which point purchasing will halt, according to its CEO.

Chart analysts also express concern, pointing to a potential head-and-shoulders pattern in Ethereum’s price chart, characterized by three peaks, with the middle peak being the highest. This pattern often signals fading buying interest, though such patterns do not always play out as expected.

At this point, it doesn’t seem so yet. The ETH/BTC ratio fell in the past week, investor money has left Ethereum ETFs for nine straight days, and the most consistent buyer is nearing its buying limit. While Lee may be outlining a future shift that could unfold over several quarters, the current data does not support this assertion.

A critical test will occur when BitMine exhausts the remaining 77,442 ETH of room under its 5% cap. If the ETH/BTC ratio stays above 0.0300 after that point, it could indicate new buyers are entering the market, bolstering Lee’s case.

Positive trends like steady ETF inflows, sustained interest in altcoins , and tokenized stocks significantly surpassing the current $3.9 billion market could lend substantial support to Lee’s case. Conversely, if the ratio dips below 0.0300 after BitMine steps back, it suggests that Ethereum’s long-term decline may still dominate the market narrative.

Shares of Strive Inc. (ASST) gained 0.76% in overnight trading late Tuesday after the company announced it will offer 5,000,000 shares of its 15% Series A Perpetual SATS Preferred Stock in an initial public offering.

The company said it will use the proceeds to acquire Bitcoin (BTC) and bitcoin-related products, fund working capital requirements, and for other general corporate purposes. The company could also use the proceeds to fund acquisitions of businesses, assets, or technologies.

The company also said it plans to establish a dividend reserve equal to 18 months of dividend payments, amounting to $22.50 per share, funded through existing cash and securities.
Strive added that it will retain the right to redeem all outstanding SATS stock if the total shares outstanding fall below 25% of the total originally issued, or upon certain tax events.

sources.title: Bitcoin (BTC) treasury news: Strive (ASST) aims to raise $500 million with SATS preferred offering - CoinDesk
passages: Bitcoin treasury company Strive ASST $27.60 · Market Closed on Tuesday evening announced a new perpetual preferred stock , SATS, with a 15% fixed dividend.

The company is aiming to sell 5 million shares at $100 per share, for a capital raise of $500 million, with proceeds to be used to purchase additional bitcoin BTC $83,498.63 , acquire income-producing assets, or buy back stock.
Unlike most bitcoin treasury companies, including far larger peer Strategy, Strive has in recent weeks been able to significantly increase its bitcoin holdings.
At closing of the offering, the company intends to establish a dividend reserve equal to the first 18 months of dividend payments on SATS.
The new share class will sit junior to Strive’s current perpetual preferred, SATA, which has a variable rate (currently 13%).
Like SATA, SATS will pay dividends on a daily basis.

sources.title: Apple’s HomeView ad is confusing to everyone except parents
passages: Apple’s ad introducing its new HomeView smart display is a little unusual.

Even if Apple didn’t need to do much to heighten the stakes of a family getting out the door, there is of course plenty of sleight of hand at work when it comes to making the HomeView appear so essential.

There’s also a microdrama about the daughter’s ride to school with a boyfriend nobody knew about that ends with everyone gathered around the HomeView watching the security camera feed of the two of them departing the porch.

When tech analyst Benedict Evans posted about the ad feeling stressful and confusing, CNET editor at large Bridget Carey chimed in to defend it, saying “It was exactly what my morning is like and it was the most real ad I’ve ever seen from Apple.” Others agreed, saying it “accurately captured” real life and that it “hit home,” no pun intended, at least I think.
Apple’s typical vibe is clean, simple, orderly; this commercial is chaos.

If the alternative is five people all interacting with their own phones, then the HomeView presents a different picture where everyone gets the essential information they need from one shared screen and stays more present.
Is the HomeView going to be enough to convince families to put their personal devices down?

extraction.body: Apple’s ad introducing its new HomeView smart display is a little unusual. It’s fast-paced and unruly, depicting a family of five as they rush through the morning routine. Apple’s typical vibe is clean, simple, orderly; this commercial is chaos. There’s also a microdrama about the daughter’s ride to school with a boyfriend nobody knew about that ends with everyone gathered around the HomeView watching the security camera feed of the two of them departing the porch. If I know anything, though, I know to trust my colleague Jen Tuohy, senior reviewer and parent to two teens, on matters of the home. “The most unrealistic part of the video is that no one is holding an iPhone.” Other parents of teens shared similar reactions on Threads. When tech analyst Benedict Evans posted about the ad feeling stressful and confusing, CNET editor at large Bridget Carey chimed in to defend it, saying “It was exactly what my morning is like and it was the most real ad I’ve ever seen from Apple.” Others agreed, saying it “accurately captured” real life and that it “hit home,” no pun intended, at least I think. Even if Apple didn’t need to do much to heighten the stakes of a family getting out the door, there is of course plenty of sleight of hand at work when it comes to making the HomeView appear so essential. The family has seemingly drilled a hole directly into the middle of their kitchen island to accommodate the charging cable, for one. And what sibling is going to check a text message from a secret boyfriend on the communal kitchen screen with their brother sitting at arm’s length? This is a far cry from the quiet luxury lifestyle everyone seems to enjoy in Apple’s Vision Pro ads. There’s also Evans’ observation that the HomeView doesn’t really solve any of the problems that come up throughout the course of the video. In the case of a spontaneous FaceTime call from the grandparents, the screen in the middle of the kitchen seems to make things worse. But maybe morning chaos isn’t the problem that’s being solved. If the alternative is five people all interacting with their own phones, then the HomeView presents a different picture where everyone gets the essential information they need from one shared screen and stays more present. A screen that makes you be more present is a lovely idea, but the real test will come when it’s in real households. Is the HomeView going to be enough to convince families to put their personal devices down? Will everyone just ignore it and keep scrolling on their own iPhones? In any case, an ungovernable morning routine is probably a feature of a busy household, not a bug.

When tech analyst Benedict Evans posted about the ad feeling stressful and confusing, CNET editor at large Bridget Carey chimed in to defend it, saying “It was exactly what my morning is like and it was the most real ad I’ve ever seen from Apple.” Others agreed, saying it “accurately captured” real life and that it “hit home,” no pun intended, at least I think. Even if Apple didn’t need to do much to heighten the stakes of a family getting out the door, there is of course plenty of sleight of hand at work when it comes to making the HomeView appear so essential. The family has seemingly drilled a hole directly into the middle of their kitchen island to accommodate the charging cable, for one. And what sibling is going to check a text message from a secret boyfriend on the communal kitchen screen with their brother sitting at arm’s length? This is a far cry from the quiet luxury lifestyle everyone seems to enjoy in Apple’s Vision Pro ads. There’s also Evans’ observation that the HomeView doesn’t really solve any of the problems that come up throughout the course of the video. In the case of a spontaneous FaceTime call from the grandparents, the screen in the middle of the kitchen seems to make things worse. But maybe morning chaos isn’t the problem that’s being solved. If the alternative is five people all interacting with their own phones, then the HomeView presents a different picture where everyone gets the essential information they need from one shared screen and stays more present. A screen that makes you be more present is a lovely idea, but the real test will come when it’s in real households. Is the HomeView going to be enough to convince families to put their personal devices down? Will everyone just ignore it and keep scrolling on their own iPhones? In any case, an ungovernable morning routine is probably a feature of a busy household, not a bug.

extraction.body: Apple today announced HomeView, a $299 smart home display with a 7-inch screen that lets users control connected accessories, make FaceTime calls, and enjoy music and video content. But what about third-party apps? Here’s what Apple says. Apple says the new HomeView smart home display is “designed for life at home,” with a wide range of features for managing connected accessories, staying organized, and enjoying entertainment. That includes everything from controlling smart home devices and checking calendars to watching videos, listening to music, and making FaceTime calls. However, one question Apple’s announcement didn’t fully answer is the extent to which HomeView will support third-party apps. According to Apple, in addition to a selection of Apple apps, including Music, Podcasts, and Safari, HomeView will also support “compatible third-party audio and video apps from your iPhone for a familiar experience across devices.” Interestingly, the fine print for this feature differs between Apple’s HomeView marketing page and the product’s press release. The press release , however, includes an additional detail (emphasis ours): Subscription may be required to access some content and services. Some applications are not available in all areas. Select apps require a paired and compatible iPhone nearby. Some of Apple’s own first-party apps will also be available from the iPhone, the company notes. That includes Audiobooks, Apple Music Classical, News, and TV. Apple has yet to detail how the iPhone proximity requirement will work, and whether developers of apps in supported categories will need to take any additional steps to support HomeView. Not trying to be the negative Nancy here but does this actually look like a useful product that will sell much outside of the apple customer that needs to get anything they put out? I know some have talked in the past about wanting something in the kitchen but what does this do that an iPad can't do for those needs? If this came out 15+ years ago, I could see it catching on for awhile before people realized they could get other devices to do what it does better. Apple is usually good with knowing their markets so I guess we'll see. This just feels like it's going against the direction of everything else. Most desktop computer users went to laptops, tablets, and phones already meaning having a static device and going mobile...or so I thought. According ot Wired , “a handful of third-party media apps like Spotify are available, and developers can bring over existing CarPlay apps.” Wired adds that “if your iPhone already has one of these CarPlay apps installed, it can automatically appear on the HomeView after setup.” So it looks like HomeView’s third-party app support will rely on the existing CarPlay framework, rather than requiring developers to build apps specifically for the device. It remains unclear, though, whether this will extend to other CarPlay app categories, such as communication and AI assistants, or also be limited to media apps. We have reached out to Apple for clarification on how third-party app support will work, and will update this post if we hear back. Are you getting an Apple HomeView? Let us know in the comments. Apple says the new HomeView smart home display is “designed for life at home,” with a wide range of features for managing connected accessories, staying organized, and enjoying entertainment. That includes everything from controlling smart home devices and checking calendars to watching videos, listening to music, and making FaceTime calls. However, one question Apple’s announcement didn’t fully answer is the extent to which HomeView will support third-party apps. According to Apple, in addition to a selection of Apple apps, including Music, Podcasts, and Safari, HomeView will also support “compatible third-party audio and video apps from your iPhone for a familiar experience across devices.” Interestingly, the fine print for this feature differs between Apple’s HomeView marketing page and the product’s press release. The press release , however, includes an additional detail (emphasis ours): Subscription may be required to access some content and services. Some applications are not available in all areas. Select apps require a paired and compatible iPhone nearby. Some of Apple’s own first-party apps will also be available from the iPhone, the company notes. That includes Audiobooks, Apple Music Classical, News, and TV. Apple has yet to detail how the iPhone proximity requirement will work, and whether developers of apps in supported categories will need to take any additional steps to support HomeView. Not trying to be the negative Nancy here but does this actually look like a useful product that will sell much outside of the apple customer that needs to get anything they put out? I know some have talked in the past about wanting something in the kitchen but what does this do that an iPad can't do for those needs? If this came out 15+ years ago, I could see it catching on for awhile before people realized they could get other devices to do what it does better. Apple is usually good with knowing their markets so I guess we'll see. This just feels like it's going against the direction of everything else. Most desktop computer users went to laptops, tablets, and phones already meaning having a static device and going mobile...or so I thought. According ot Wired , “a handful of third-party media apps like Spotify are available, and developers can bring over existing CarPlay apps.” Wired adds that “if your iPhone already has one of these CarPlay apps installed, it can automatically appear on the HomeView after setup.” So it looks like HomeView’s third-party app support will rely on the existing CarPlay framework, rather than requiring developers to build apps specifically for the device. It remains unclear, though, whether this will extend to other CarPlay app categories, such as communication and AI assistants, or also be limited to media apps. We have reached out to Apple for clarification on how third-party app support will work, and will update this post if we hear back. Are you getting an Apple HomeView? Let us know in the comments.
